Second, to clarify the differences in the stages of the three vehicles within the Tripiṭaka Teaching,
there are three points.
First, the stage of the Śrāvaka vehicle is clarified;
second, the stage of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle is clarified;
third, the stage of the Bodhisattva vehicle is clarified.
First, regarding the stages of the Śrāvaka vehicle within the Tripiṭaka teaching:
the Tripiṭaka teaching as a whole possesses four gates;
here, the explanation is specifically based on the "existence" (bhāva) gate of the Abhidharma.
Next, below, there is a separate brief explanation of the stages (*bhūmi*) by way of the gate of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
Regarding the explanation of the stages by way of the gate of existence (*bhava*), there are two points:
first, the explanation of the seven stages of the noble seekers (*saptakalyāṇapudgala*).
Second, the clarification of the seven stages of the noble ones (*ārya*).
First, the clarification of the seven stages of the worthy ones (*pṛthagjana*) consists of:
first, the contemplation of the five objects for settling the mind (*pañca-viṣaya-sthiti-citta-bhāvanā*).
Second, the four applications of mindfulness through distinct contemplation;
third, the four applications of mindfulness through collective contemplation;
fourth, the stage of "heat" (*uṣmagata*).
Fifth, the stage of the summit;
sixth, the stage of patience;
seventh, the stage of the supreme mundane dharma.
These constitute the seven stages of the worthy ones (*saptakula-putra*).
Generally speaking, one is called "worthy" (*bhadra*) because they are adjacent to the sages (*ārya*).

These seven stages are all instances of conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) that is neither of the learner (śaikṣa) nor of the non-learner (aśaikṣa), which, through their semblance of understanding,
are able to suppress the afflictions of the views (dṛṣṭikleśa).
Therefore, because this semblance-understanding can give rise to the true illumination of the patience toward suffering (*duḥkha-kṣānti*),
it is said that those adjacent to the sages are called "Worthy Ones" (*bhadra*).
Now, "Worthy One" (*xian*) is interpreted as meaning "direct goodness."
All the celestial Māras and their retinues, as well as all ordinary worldlings,
cultivate goodness with a mind of attachment.
All non-Buddhists cultivate goodness with a mind of false views.
Although these individuals may practice virtue,
their conduct is hypocritical and crooked, and thus cannot be called straightforward.
Now, among the disciples of the Buddha, there are seven types of practitioners.
They all clearly understood the principle of the Four Noble Truths regarding arising and ceasing;
they knew that the theories of craving and views were both deviant and crooked,
and they subdued this deviant and crooked mind of craving and views.
Because one cultivates all wholesome dharmas with right faith and a straightforward mind,
it is called "straightforward wholesomeness" (*ṛju-kuśala*).
Furthermore, it is that which is elucidated by all treatises on love (*vātsalya*).
All possess the principle of arising and ceasing,
yet this is invisible to the celestial Māras and their retinues,
as well as to all ordinary beings.
Therefore, the cycle of birth and death revolves like a wheel.
Furthermore, all that is expounded by the various philosophical views contains the principle of the Four Noble Truths regarding arising and ceasing.
The six heretical teachers were all unable to perceive it.
Therefore, one wanders through birth and death like a revolving wheel.
Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
In the past, you and I did not see the Four Noble Truths;
for this reason, we have long wandered through the great ocean of suffering in saṃsāra.
Now, within the Buddha-dharma, there are seven types of practitioners.
From hearing, understanding arises; through this clear understanding, one recognizes these two types of arising and ceasing within the Four Noble Truths.
Consequently, one attains upright faith.
With this upright mind, one cultivates all wholesome dharmas.
Because they are straightforwardly virtuous, they are collectively termed "worthy ones" (*bhadra*).
Question: Why are they said to belong to the principle of the Four Noble Truths, which involve arising and ceasing through craving?
The answer is:
The karmic retribution of a practitioner for a single lifetime is precisely the fruit belonging to craving.
Because it possesses the three types of suffering, it is called "suffering" (*duḥkha*).
Because the principle of suffering is examined and found to be real and not false, it is termed a "truth" (*satya*).
Regarding this fruit of suffering:
Due to ignorance and a lack of understanding, one becomes attached to these fruits and gives rise to various evil karmas,
which are capable of summoning and accumulating the retribution of intense suffering in the three miserable realms.
Furthermore, through attachment to these fruits, one gives rise to various wholesome karmas that can summon and accumulate the retributions of birth and death among asuras, humans, and devas.
These two types of bound karma—
That which can summon the retributive suffering of birth and death within the twenty-five states of existence across the six realms is collectively termed "Accumulation" (samudaya).
Because the principle of accumulation is examined with precision and is not false, it is designated as a "Truth" (satya).
If one can contemplate this reward body (saṃbhogakāya) and cultivate the precepts,
meditative concentration, and wisdom— the four foundations of mindfulness and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment—
thereby reaching nirvāṇa, this is termed the Path.
That which is examined and verified through principle is called *satya* (truth).
Belonging to the afflictions of craving and the karma of good and evil,
the cessation of the causes of the twenty-five states of existence within the three realms is termed the "extinction of the bonds of the son."
Having cast off this retribution body,
one shall never again undergo the bitter fruits of the twenty-five states of existence within the triple world;
this is called the extinction of the bondage of the fruit.
These two kinds of cessation are called "cessation.
Because the principle of cessation is examined and verified, it is called "truth" (*satya*). Question:
What is meant by "the principle of the Four Truths belonging to arising and ceasing as perceived by views"?
The answer is:
the retribution-body (*vipākakāya*) of sentient beings for the duration of one lifetime.
That which possesses the three types of suffering is called "suffering" (duḥkha).
Because the principle of suffering is examined and found to be real and not false, it is called a "truth" (satya).
One is deluded regarding this retribution body.
The two views, four views, and sixty-two views that arise from within oneself are precisely ignorance,
craving, and grasping. Because of these,
if one gives rise to unwholesome karma, [it follows].
Thus, one can summon and accumulate the retributive suffering of the three miserable realms;
furthermore, if one gives rise to wholesome karma on this basis,
one can summon and accumulate the fruits of birth and death as an asura, human, or deva.

These two types of fetters and karma are able to summon and accumulate the fruits of birth-and-death suffering within the six realms, the three worlds, and the twenty-five states of existence; therefore,
they are collectively termed "accumulation" (samudaya).
Because they are gathered together, their principle is examined and found to be real and not false; thus they are called "truths" (*satya*).
If one can contemplate these various views as defilements—the five aggregates (*skandha*), both wholesome and unwholesome—[one attains liberation].
Cultivating the precepts, concentration, wisdom, the four foundations of mindfulness, and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment enables one to reach Nirvana; this is called the Path (*mārga*).
Because its principles are examined, real, and not false, it is called the Truth (*satya*).
If the two views of self-identity and extremes are extinguished,
then all eighty-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), afflictions, and karmas are extinguished,
and one attains the fruit of *srotāpanna*.
When one who has transcended [the world] contemplates the ten fetters (*daśa-anuśaya*) within the three realms and brings them to cessation,
then the ninety-eight fetters, karmas, and afflictions (*kleśa*) are extinguished.

This is called the extinction of the cause of the twenty-five states of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*) within the three realms, which is termed the extinction of the bonds of the son (*putra-bandhana*).
Having abandoned these karmic retributions,
one ultimately does not give rise to the fruits of bondage known as the twenty-five existences within the three realms;
the cessation of these two types is what is called "cessation."
The principle of cessation, being examined and verified as real, is termed a "truth" (satya).
Herein we clarify that these various views regarding the Four Truths are all the subjects of discourse in the degenerate age, concerning which Dīrghanakha was deluded.
To explain the names and meanings of the Four Noble Truths horizontally ensures a thorough and detailed understanding of their reality;
however, to clarify them vertically does not necessarily allow for a profound insight into this meaning.
Therefore, what was erroneous is taken as correct.
Taking the correct for the erroneous;
taking the shallow for the profound;
and taking the profound for the shallow.
Worldly and world-transcending dharmas are intermingled and indistinguishable.
Whether listening to lectures or practicing seated meditation,
if one clearly understands this meaning, [one will not be deluded].
Thereupon, he attained clear and distinct right faith in the Buddha-dharma,
took refuge in the Triple Gem,
and the aspiration for the Way arose spontaneously within him.
They single-mindedly seek nirvana, free from suffering;
they never become stained by or attached to words and language, nor to useless disputations,
nor to worldly fame, profit, kinship, or karmic rewards.
Of these seven types of worthy ones,
three are external ordinary beings and are called the Stage of Dry Wisdom;
the fourth is an internal ordinary being and is the Stage of Nature.
If those prior to the stage of external ordinary beings (bāhyapṛthagjana) have not necessarily been able to take refuge in the Triple Gem,
how could they recognize the Four Noble Truths through desire and views, or practice the five stabilizing minds (pañca-smṛtyupasthāna)?
They are all termed sentient beings of the group fixed in error (mithyātva-niyata-rāśi).
If those at the stage of "dry wisdom" (śuklavidarśanā-bhūmi) are called beings of the indeterminate group (aniyata-rāśi),
then those at the stage of "nature" (gotra-bhūmi) are called beings of the right-determinate group (samyaktva-niyata-rāśi).
First, to clarify the five stopping-minds contemplations (pañca-vyupaśama-citta-vidarśanā) of the first noble person (ārya-pudgala):
First, the contemplation of ānāpāna;
second, the contemplation of impurity;
third, the contemplation of loving-kindness.
The contemplation of the four causal conditions and the contemplation of the skillful means regarding the five elements—
these five are collectively termed "stabilizing the mind."
"Stopping" (ting) takes the meaning of cessation.
It is also called the "Contemplation of the Five Degrees Gate.
If a person takes refuge in the Triple Gem and receives the Buddha's precepts, [they may practice this].
They are called the fourfold assembly of the Buddha's disciples;
if they hear the teaching of the Four Noble Truths regarding arising and ceasing,
they thereby give rise to the mind of a śrāvaka.
If one wishes to contemplate the Four Noble Truths in order to leave behind the suffering of birth and death and seek the bliss of Nirvana,
yet these [truths] are unsettled and distracted by the five kinds of afflictions like a lamp in the wind,
one should cultivate the five kinds of contemplative methods.
The five kinds of contemplative methods are:
first, the contemplation of counting the breath;
second, the contemplation of impurity.
3. Contemplation of the mind of loving-kindness;
4. Contemplation of causes and conditions; 5.
Contemplation of the skillful means regarding the elements.
Question:
Why does one not rely on the Sāṃkhya school’s teaching that the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) must come first? Answer:
Now, I shall distinguish the sequence according to the Chan gate.
Since the progression of ailments varies according to the individual,
there is no need to rigidly adhere to a fixed order of priority.
Question:
Do these five methods of contemplation apply to five different types of persons, or do they apply to a single person?
The answer is:
horizontally it corresponds to five people; vertically it corresponds to one person;
as for the single person, it corresponds to an indefinite number according to the extent of their illness.
These five methods of contemplation serve as antidotes to the five unwholesome states;
thus, there are five intentions.
1. Counteracting; 2. Transformative counteracting;
3. Non-counteracting;
4. Simultaneous counteracting.
The fifth [category] is both an object of counteraction and a turning away;
it is also non-turning and serves as a combined remedy.
Regarding the first type of counteraction:
If discursive thought (*vitarka*) and sustained reflection (*vicāra*) are excessive,
one should apply the antidote of counting the breaths (*ānāpānagaṇanā*). If the two types of sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*) are excessive, [one should apply their respective antidotes].
To counteract impurity,
and for those with an abundance of ill will,
one should cultivate loving-kindness as the antidote.
Fourth, for those with an abundance of delusion,
the antidote is the cultivation of the contemplation of causes and conditions.
Fifth, for those with an abundance of attachment to a self—
Regarding the cultivation of the elements as a skillful means for remediation:
if a practitioner’s afflictions of vitarka and vicāra are equally weighted and predominate such that the mind cannot remain fixed on its object,
they should practice counting the breaths.
Contemplating the breath in accordance with the breath serves as an antidote;
when it is properly applied, the three types of discursive thought and afflictions are stilled,
and the mind, no longer wavering or distracted, gives rise to various meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*).
Because one enters and exits with a concentrated mind through the power of meditative absorption (samādhi),
it is called "stabilizing the mind. Why is this so?
There are three types of meditative concentration on mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasmṛti):
first, that of initial practice;
second, that of practiced mastery.
The third is called "having transcended through reflection.
First, counting is the initial practice;
second, following is the practice once it has been mastered.
Once the three contemplations have been mastered,
the subsequent counting and following-contemplations are all termed "initial practice.
Through this practice, one attains the three types of *anāgamya* (unattained) concentration of the desire realm.
This is called "having practiced the conduct.
The arising of the various initial dhyāna concentrations is called "having crossed over.
As for the remaining four methods of stabilizing the mind, such as the contemplation of impurity and so forth:
One should also distinguish [the mind] in this manner.
Once the mind is stabilized, one may then practice contemplation,
like a lamp in a sealed room.
There is no method for entering the Way that surpasses these five dharmas.
If the mind does not abide,
one must apply corrective measures— whether through active transformation or non-transformation— and thereby give rise to the merits of the various dhyānas.
This is fully explained in the "Expedient Means" section within the *Cidi Chanmen* (The Gate of Sequential Meditation).
When a practitioner successfully accomplishes one contemplation and their mind attains stability,
they immediately enter the stage of the first noble person (*ārya*).
Question: Why is it that in this section the Buddha-recollection samādhi (buddhānusmṛti-samādhi) is not explained as being of five kinds?
The answer is:
To open the contemplation of causes and conditions is to give rise to the skillful means of the realm of beings as a substitute.
The skillful means regarding the realms (*dhātu*) is the same as the Small Vehicle’s mindfulness of the Buddhas;
it also destroys the obstacle of being oppressed by objective spheres. Some say:
If one establishes the framework of the five perfections, there is no mention of the name of mindfulness of the Buddha;
if one establishes the framework of the six perfections,
it then clarifies the perfection of mindfulness of the Buddha.
This cures the obstacles of the path that arise from [the imbalance of] the elements.
A question is asked:
"If the mind can be made to abide through methods such as counting the breath or [contemplating] impurity," [how is this so?].
As for the first type of worthy person:
those in the present age who practice contemplations such as counting the breath or the foul are not merely abiding in the mind.
One then gives rise to various meditative states (*dhyāna-mukha-viṣaya*).
Is this the stage of the first *ārya*?
The answer is: No.
If one cultivates the first dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception with a mind of craving and views,
it is not even the first stage of worthiness.
How much more so for those whose minds cannot remain still even during practices such as counting the breath or the meditation on impurity,
yet who give rise to shallow and mundane meditative absorptions (dhyāna) and call themselves "worthy ones" (ārya). Why is this?
As stated in the sutras,
one who extensively cultivates merit and meditative concentration but does not cultivate wisdom is called a fool.
To cultivate wisdom extensively while failing to cultivate merit, meditative concentration,
and dhyāna is called madness.
How could one describe such a mad and foolish person as a "primary worthy"?
Now it is clear that the worthy one was originally but an upright and virtuous person.
[The interlocutor] asks:
What are the characteristics of an upright and virtuous person?
The answer is:
This should be distinguished according to four meanings.
First, if a person violates the precepts due to attachment or wrong views.
Because this is neither upright nor virtuous, one is not a worthy person;
like a person without eyes or feet,
they cannot reach the pond of cool purity.
Second, there are those who maintain the precepts and practice meditative concentration yet give rise to false views;
such goodness is not upright, and they cannot be called virtuous.
It is like having feet but lacking eyes.
Nor can they reach the Lake of Coolness.
Third, those who have given rise to faith and right view but whose minds are distracted by a violation of the precepts—
this is simply unwholesome.
Nor can they be called wise;
like those who have eyes but no feet,
they likewise cannot reach the Pool of Coolness.
Fourth, if a person possesses faith and understanding, directly and correctly grasps the intent of the Buddha’s teaching,
maintains pure ethical discipline, and cultivates practices such as *ānāpāna-smṛti* (mindfulness of breathing) and the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*),
they will attain mental stability.
This is called the station of the first noble one of upright goodness.
Just as a person who is complete in both eyes and feet may enter the cool pond.
Question:
What is meant by "faithful understanding that is direct and correct," which consists in discerning the characteristics of the intended meaning of the Buddha’s teachings?
The answer is:
As stated in the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*,
five hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
Among people during the period of the Semblance Dharma,
their faculties have become increasingly dull and they are deeply attached to all phenomena;
they seek the definitive characteristics of the twelve links of dependent origination, the five aggregates, the twelve bases, the eighteen elements, and so forth.
They do not understand the Buddha’s intention and merely cling to the literal words.
Regarding the statement that they do not understand the Buddha’s intention:
the Buddha knows that the arising of all things cannot be said to have causes and conditions.
Therefore, it can also be explained.
The Buddha taught the gate of the doctrine on arising through causes and conditions and cessation through causes and conditions,
in order to transform sentient beings according to their capacities.
The intention is to cause sentient beings to leave behind the suffering of birth and death and attain the bliss of nirvana.
If one becomes attached to words and engages in conceptual discrimination and contention,
one will be burned by the burning house of the three realms.
This does not grasp the Buddha’s intent.
Now, to clarify how one may know the Buddha’s intent:
if one understands the ten intents of the Three Piṭaka teachings clearly and distinctly.
One will certainly transcend the suffering of birth and death and attain the bliss of nirvana.
As for the ten points:
These are the ten dharmas;
their names and categories are fully explained as previously detailed in the section on the three contemplations.
Now, they shall be briefly interpreted according to this gateway of the Tripitaka Teaching.
First, those who believe and understand the principle of causes and conditions through right reasoning are those who know that the unspeakable is spoken as the causal condition of ignorance,
which gives rise to all phenomena.
It refutes the claims of outsiders that all phenomena arise without causes and conditions;
it refutes the claims of outsiders that all phenomena arise from false causes and conditions—
namely, their various inverted, deluded, and deviant conceptualizations.
Second, as for those who have truly resolved their minds:
they are startled awake by the fire of impermanence burning through all worlds,
and with single-minded devotion, they joyfully seek nirvana.
He does not dwell upon worldly fame, reputation, profit,
or sustenance, like a deer within a hunting net longing to leap out.
Third, he skillfully cultivates śamatha and vipaśyanā.
The practitioner who has transcended the world is like a person riding a horse who also loves to spur it on.
Fourth, the universal penetration of all phenomena.
Contemplating the arising and ceasing of causes and conditions,
one shatters all attachments, views, and conceptual proliferations regarding all phenomena.
Fifth, being well-acquainted with what is open and what is obstructed.
To know that all phenomena of craving and views possess the principle of their cessation through the Path is called "penetration";
to know that they all possess suffering and its accumulation is called "obstruction."
Regarding the sixth, the adept cultivation of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment that brings about composure:
one remains unmoved by various cravings and views while cultivating the foundations of mindfulness and the eightfold noble path.
The seventh, the skillful cultivation of the factors that assist the path,
consists of cultivating the five faiths,
entering the twelve gates of dhyāna, the nine notions, and the eight liberations.

It refers to the various wholesome remedial dharmas that aid the path of contemplation, such as the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) and the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*),
which one enters deeply and contemplates together. Eighth,
"skillfully knowing the sequence of stages" means skillfully recognizing the seven stages of the spiritual nobles (*saptakula-ārya*) so that the mind does not become confused or muddled.
This refers to the Sangha who have destroyed overweening pride and have achieved a sense of shame,
remorse, and modesty. Ninth,
those who have accomplished patient endurance are able to endure the two types of thieves— internal and external— the three obstacles, and the four māras.

Regarding the non-arising of craving for the ten dharmas conducive to the Path: this refers to the practitioner not feeling attachment in their mind toward the various wholesome dharmas conducive to the Path belonging to both the outer and inner ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
This concerns practitioners of the Śrāvaka vehicle in the final age.
Knowing these ten dharmas with clear faith and understanding,
one does not cling to any verbal proliferation of letters;
seeking true wisdom, one practices the five methods of mental abiding (*pañca-vipaśyanā-sthiti*).
Entering the first stage of the noble ones (*ārya*) constitutes the thorough knowledge of the intent of the Buddha’s teaching.
Second, the explanation of the stage of the four applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) with distinct conceptualizations:
This constitutes seven points.
First is the elucidation of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*),
which are the essential gateways for entering the path in the Buddha-dharma.
First, a brief explanation of the names of the four foundations of mindfulness;
second, a detailed differentiation of the three types of foundations of mindfulness;
third, an elucidation of how they serve to refute the three types of six teachers.
The fifth elucidates the three types of arhats;
the sixth elucidates the method of observing the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna);
and the seventh correctly elucidates the stages of the foundations of mindfulness.
First, to clarify that the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) are the essential gateway for entering the path of the Buddha-dharma:
when the Buddha was between the twin trees, about to enter parinirvāṇa,
Ānanda asked him a question.
After the Buddha has passed into parinirvāṇa,
upon what shall the bhikṣus rely for their dwelling and upon what shall they rely to cultivate the path?
The Buddha answered Ānanda:
Whether I am in the world or have entered parinirvāṇa,
if the bhikṣus rely upon the prātimokṣa,
abide in the foundations of mindfulness, and cultivate the path.
One should know that when the five contemplations for settling the mind (*pañca-viṣaya-sthāpana*) are accomplished, one enters the first stage of the noble ones (*ārya*).
This is based upon the purity of ethical discipline (*śīla*),
which is termed the precept of restraining the sense faculties (*indriya-saṃvara-śīla*).
Therefore, the Sāṃkhyas describe the desire-realm concentration (*kāmadhātu-samādhi*) as being associated with the ten wholesome courses of action (*daśakuśala-karmapatha*).
If one relies on the stage of "not yet arrived" (*anāgamya-bhūmi*), [it is likewise so].
The arising of the first dhyāna is itself the precept associated with meditative concentration (samādhi-saṃvara).
Although the Buddha-dharma contains various gateways to the Dharma,
the Buddha’s final instruction states:
This refers solely to cultivating the path by relying on the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna).
If one is separated from the foundations of mindfulness,
then even if one practices giving, ethical discipline, patience, and diligence through contemplation, [it is not the true path].
Whether reciting sutras, practicing the path, observing the dhūta ascetic practices, sitting in meditation,
listening to teachings, reading extensively, or lecturing and transforming others through instruction—
none of these can lead one into the True Path.
Therefore, the Buddha exhorted [practitioners] to cultivate the path by relying on the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
Second, to briefly explain the names of the four foundations of mindfulness:
the four foundations of mindfulness are also called "appropriate abidings" (*yoniśo-sthiti*).
This is precisely the contemplation of the body, sensation, mind, and phenomena within each of the five aggregates, twelve bases, and eighteen elements among all dharmas.
As for "true wisdom":
It is the wisdom that shatters the four dharmas, the four inversions, the four nutriments, the four consciousnesses, the four abodes, and the four māras.
First is the foundation of mindfulness of the body;
second is the foundation of mindfulness of sensation.
The three foundations of mindfulness of mind and the four foundations of mindfulness of phenomena.
Regarding the foundation of mindfulness of the body:
All internal and external aggregates of form are called the body.
The wisdom that contemplates the body is called mindfulness.
Clearly seeing impurity destroys the perversion of perceiving purity.
This is termed a "foundation" (āyatana);
this constitutes the foundation of mindfulness of the body.
Second is the foundation of mindfulness of feelings (vedanā-smṛtyupasthāna).
All internal and external aggregates of sensation are called "sensation.
The wisdom that contemplates sensation is called "mindfulness.
To know that all sensations are suffering and to shatter the perversion of regarding them as pleasure [is mindfulness].
This is designated as a "foundation" (āyatana).
This is called the foundation of mindfulness of feeling (vedanā-smṛtyupasthāna).
All internal and external aggregates of consciousness are called the mind (*citta*).
The wisdom that contemplates the mind is called mindfulness (*smṛti*).
It perceives that all minds are impermanent, thereby shattering the perversion of permanence.
This is called a "foundation" (āyatana);
this is what is meant by the foundation of mindfulness of the mind.
As for the four foundations of mindfulness of phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna):
All internal and external perceptions and formations— the two aggregates—
as well as all conditioned phenomena, are termed "dharmas.
Wisdom is termed "mindfulness" (smṛti).
To perceive the selflessness of phenomena (dharmanairātmya) and thereby destroy the inversion of a self is called the "foundation" (sthāna).
This is the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna);
these are the four foundations of mindfulness.
There are twelve kinds of contemplation, namely:
four internal, four external, and four internal-external.
Question:
The four foundations of mindfulness are wisdom.
Why, then, are they designated by the name "mindfulness"?
The answer is:
For the sake of beginners, it employs mindfulness, retention, and wisdom;
because it takes non-delusory attention to diverse objects as its predominant factor,
it derives its name from "mindfulness" (smṛti).
Regarding the analysis of the three types of foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) according to the Threefold Clarification:
first, the foundation of mindfulness of intrinsic nature;
second, the shared foundation of mindfulness.
The three foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
Regarding what is called the foundation of mindfulness as intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-smṛtyupasthāna*):
it refers to non-erroneous wisdom (*aviparīta-prajñā*). As the Buddha said, "One who cultivates the contemplation of the body, contemplating the body, possesses wisdom."
Regarding the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*):
because one does not falsely grasp at the conditions for the activities performed,
the faults of their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) are eliminated.
Therefore, it is called the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna).
Master Nanyue said that they are also called the practice of wisdom (prajñācaryā).
It is also called "contemplation of reality" (yathābhūta-pratyavekṣā),
the essential method for severing the fetters by taking principle as its object.
As for what is called the "shared foundations of mindfulness" (sāmānya-smṛtyupasthāna):
Concentration and wisdom are co-existent dharmas.
As the Buddha said, when a bhikṣu accumulates wholesome dharmas,
it is correctly stated that these are the four foundations of mindfulness.
The Master of Nanyue said:
"It is also called 'the practice of practices' and it is also called 'contemplation that attains understanding.'"
This refers to the wholesome dharmas within the context of the remedies;
together with the Noble Path, they sever the fetters, form, and all numerical categories.
Furthermore, they are capable of giving rise to the various supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
Regarding what is called the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*):
as the Buddha has taught, monks, all phenomena are the four foundations of mindfulness.
This is for the sake of being fully and correctly sustained,
and because it is a brief object of focus.
Master Nanyue said:
Alternatively, there are two kinds of foundations of mindfulness:
those of nature and those of commonality. These combine the observing wisdom and the observed objects to fully encompass the meaning of all phenomena.
If one is able to discern and observe [these],
one immediately gives rise to the four kinds of unhindered eloquence (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ*). Question:
As stated in the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*:
"The afflictions are abandoned by means of the [four] foundations of mindfulness taken together,
not by the foundations of mindfulness in their individual natures."
Although there is a brief object of focus,
it is not complete and thus cannot sever the fetters.
He replied:
The faculties of sentient beings are either sharp or dull.
Those with dull faculties have thick fetters; they cannot sever these fetters even if they do not possess the auxiliary paths.
Those with sharp faculties have thin fetters; although they may not possess the auxiliary paths, [they can still sever them].
The wisdom of the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) is itself capable of severing the fetters (saṃyojana).
Furthermore, as explained in the *Abhidharma-hṛdaya*, it is the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna) that severs the fetters.
This is not the same as the first three foundations of mindfulness;
it is now explained according to what is taught in the *Dhyāna-sūtra*,
where Mahākātyāyana established the foundation of mindfulness of the body.
If contemplation is perfected, one immediately attains the first fruit [of the path].
Why must it necessarily reach the stage of the foundation of mindfulness of dharmas?
Question: Regarding the foundation of mindfulness of nature (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna):
It is only said that the faculty of wisdom is weak;
how then can it sever the fetters?
The answer is: the faculty of wisdom does not arise alone.
"How could one not be able to sever the fetters?
[The interlocutor] asks:
"If the various mental formations arise in succession,"
This is precisely the meaning of "commonality.
The answer states:
There are two types of numerical designations that arise accordingly.
First, when the wisdom that contemplates principles arises spontaneously and in accordance with various numerical categories,
this is called the application of mindfulness to nature (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*).
Second, by practicing various meditative counts (*gaṇanā*) as auxiliary wholesome dharmas for the path,
one abandons the fetters through the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
Therefore, the Buddha spoke of the accumulation of wholesome dharmas.
This pertains to the applications of mindfulness in common (*sāmānya-smṛtyupasthāna*),
because they assist the Noble Path in collectively severing the fetters and proclivities (*saṃyojana-anuśaya*).
The *Saṃyuktābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* specifically states that it is through the applications of mindfulness in common that the fetters are severed.
However, for those of sharp faculties, the application of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) does not mean that the fetters (*saṃyojana*) are not severed.

The Fourfold Clarity (*Sishiming*) states that this is because the Buddha taught the four foundations of mindfulness in order to refute the three types of six teachers; thus, this teaching on the foundations of mindfulness transcends the doctrines of those three groups of six teachers.
Therefore, one is able to defeat all non-Buddhists.
If practitioners of the Three Vehicles cultivate the three kinds of foundations of mindfulness and achieve mastery, [they likewise attain this].
It can also defeat all outsiders.
What are the three types of six teachers among the non-Buddhists?
The first is the "omniscient" six teachers.
Second, the six teachers of supernatural powers;
third, the six teachers of the Vedas;
and the six teachers of omniscience.
When one perceives principles with a deviant mind, it arises from deviant wisdom; this is unimpeded eloquence regarding phenomena.
As for the six masters of supernatural powers, they attained worldly meditative concentrations and developed the five supernormal powers.
There is also the power of compassion and patience;
whether cut by a blade or smeared with fragrance, the mind feels neither hatred nor attachment.
All of these are the functional applications of the fundamental twelve-gate dhyāna-concentration.
The six teachers of the Vedas were those who were extensively learned and possessed great erudition,
having mastered the four Vedas and the eighteen great scriptures.
He knew everything concerning the auspicious and inauspicious signs of the world, astronomy, geography, medical prescriptions, divination, and physiognomy;
therefore, he was named one of the Six Teachers of the Vedas.
Such were these six teachers.
Internally possessing all-encompassing wisdom,
he was externally able to perform supernatural transformations;
he knew the auspicious and inauspicious signs of the world and mastered the four Vedas.
Furthermore, he was thoroughly conversant with the eighteen great sūtras;
thus, each possessed wisdom, supernormal powers, and understanding.
The sixteen great kingdoms revered him as if he were a Buddha.
In order to refute these three kinds of six teachers,
these three kinds of four foundations of mindfulness are taught: first,
the foundation of mindfulness of intrinsic nature (svabhāva-smṛtyupasthāna).
This immediately refutes the six teachers who claim to possess all-knowledge. Why is this?
Because outsiders all give rise to their claims of all-knowledge based on the two views of self-identity and extremes.
This refers to attaining the permanence, bliss, self, and purity of Nirvana;
it is like a worm gnawing through a wooden puppet and accidentally forming characters—
the worm itself does not know whether these are characters or not.
Now, when the Buddha teaches the contemplation of the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna),
it immediately destroys these two views— the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) and the view of extremes (antagrāhadṛṣṭi)—
so that the four views, the sixty-two views, and all inverted perceptions do not arise.
Therefore, he refutes the six masters who [claim to] possess all-knowledge.
Next, he clarifies the common foundations of mindfulness (sāmānya-smṛtyupasthāna) to refute the six masters who [claim to] possess supernormal powers (abhijñā).
Non-Buddhists develop the five supernormal powers only within the four fundamental dhyānas;
since their meditative concentration is shallow and they lack the contemplation of both principle and phenomena, [they cannot attain liberation].
Therefore, the transformation of supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) is hardly worth mentioning. Now, when the Buddha speaks of the "shared foundations of mindfulness" (*sādhāraṇa-smṛtyupasthāna*),

it is precisely through these that one can give rise to the liberations (*vimokṣa*), the spheres of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*), the nine successive attainments (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*), the lion’s sport (*siṃhavijṛmbhita*), the leap-over (*vyutkrāntaka*), the various supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), and the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*).
Since his power from deep practice was great, the supernormal powers he manifested were unimpeded and sovereign;
his transformations were boundless, crushing all non-Buddhists as easily as looking at the palm of one's hand.
Thus, Śāriputra subdued the Raudrākṣa,
and Maudgalyāyana converted the non-Buddhists who were drowning in the river;
these were all supernormal powers accomplished through the contemplation of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).
Next, the contemplation of the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) is explained,
which refutes the Vedas and non-Buddhist outsiders.
This consists of the four Vedas and the eighteen great scriptures.
They all clarify only the mundane matters of the worldly gods and humans concerning theories of desire and views, which are shallow and superficial.
As for the supramundane Tripiṭaka taught by the Buddha—
both its names and its meanings— they are not recorded in those scriptures.
The Buddha taught the contemplation of the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna),
which takes as its object the doctrinal gates of the Tripiṭaka spoken by the Buddha,
as well as the principles of the supramundane categories of names, meanings, and dharmas.
If one compares them side by side, how could these be outside the scope of what others have seen and heard?
Therefore, the contemplation of the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) is used to refute the Vedas and the non-Buddhist outsiders.
*Sijiao yi*, fascicle four.
The Meaning of the Four Teachings, Scroll Five.
Composed by Master Zhiyi of Xiu Chan Temple on Mount Tiantai.
Regarding the five vidyās and the three types of *smṛtyupasthāna* that result in the three kinds of *arhat*: first, if one practices them singly...
The foundations of mindfulness of intrinsic nature result in an Arhat liberated by wisdom;
the two common foundations of mindfulness [result in both].
One becomes an Arhat liberated through both parts by means of three conditions;
one becomes an Arhat liberated through non-delusion by means of the foundations of mindfulness.
Why is this so? The foundations of mindfulness are themselves the wisdom that takes principle as its object.
When associated with these foundations of mindfulness, true outflow-free [wisdom] is generated.
He immediately becomes an Arhat liberated through wisdom (prajñā-vimukta).
Together with the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) and the wholesome five aggregates (pañca-skandha),
he accomplishes the liberations (vimokṣa), up to the samādhis of transcendence (abhibhvāyatana), the knowledge of vows (praṇidhi-jñāna), and the summit dhyāna (mūrdha-dhyāna).
In this way, these aids to the path, together with the true path, cause the arising of genuine outflow-free wisdom;
one immediately attains the three knowledges, the six supernormal powers, and the eight liberations,
becoming an Arhat liberated both ways.
If one takes the foundations of mindfulness as the object,
this refers to all the aggregates, bases, and elements expounded by the Buddha’s teachings;
these constitute the two types of foundations of mindfulness, namely those of nature and those of commonality.
Regarding the names and meanings of the observer and the observed:
if one contemplates these names and meanings while in meditative concentration,
one will immediately give rise to the four types of unimpeded eloquence (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ*).
He is named the Great Arhat of Unimpeded Liberation.
It is asked:
Why is he called by a name associated with wisdom?
This is indeed the Dharmaguptaka school and not that used by the Saṃmatīya school.
The answer is:
since the teachings of the Tripiṭaka are the same, there is no fault in using both.
Furthermore, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya-gāthā* states:
"It should be known that one liberated by wisdom (prajñāvimukta) does not attain the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti).
If one attains the meditative absorption of cessation..."
"One should know them as both liberated.
This verse clarifies that there are differences between those who possess wisdom at specific times and those who possess it regardless of time.
Question:
One should not speak of "unhindered liberation" separately,
as there is no such designation for the nine types of arhats.
The answer is:
This is from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
It clarifies that when the Dharma-piṭaka was to be compiled, one thousand arhats were assembled,
all of whom had attained both common liberation and unimpeded liberation.
Just as a pratyekabuddha appears in a world where no Buddha exists,
and although they attain the requisites for awakening— namely the three knowledges, the eight liberations, the six supernormal powers, and various transformations—
they do so because they have not heard the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma.
Therefore, they do not attain the four unhindered analytical knowledges;
yet, if they wish to repay the kindness of the faithful offerings,
they simply manifest the eighteen transformations.
How much more so for an Arhat who has not heard the Buddha’s teaching of the Tripiṭaka—
how could they spontaneously give rise to the four unhindered analytical knowledges to explain the Buddha-dharma without obstruction or stagnation?
Sixth, regarding the method of contemplation on the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna):
there are three types of this method of contemplation.
First is the foundation of mindfulness as intrinsic nature (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna).
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"The nature of the foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) is wisdom.
The wisdom that contemplates the body is the foundation of mindfulness of the body (*kāyasmṛtyupasthāna*)."
The same applies to feeling, mind, and mental factors (*citta-dharma*).
There are differing interpretations:
some take only the factor of wisdom (*prajñā*) to constitute the nature of wisdom (*prajñā-svabhāva*).
This is precisely the foundation of mindfulness of nature (dharmasmṛtyupasthāna).
According to the interpretation of Master Nanyue,
observing the rational nature of the five aggregates is called the foundation of mindfulness of nature.
Therefore, a verse in the *Saṃyuktābhidharmahṛdaya* says:
"This body has the characteristic of impurity;
its true nature is eternally empty."
The same is said for all feelings and mental phenomena (*cittadharma*).
Regarding the contemplation of the specific nature of the foundation of mindfulness of perceptions (*saṃjñā-smṛtyupasthāna*),
there are two ways of breaking the four inversions (*viparyāsa*).
First, the destruction of craving;
second, the destruction of views.
Regarding the first, the application of mindfulness that destroys the nature of craving:
Indeed, among all classes of living beings,
there are none who do not feel attachment to the five aggregates as the fruit of retribution,
as well as to their external environment of support.
Regarding the contemplation of the body as a foundation of mindfulness:
one contemplates this internal body as having five kinds of impurity.
First is the impurity of the place of birth.
Second, impurity of the seed;
third, impurity of specific characteristics;
fourth, impurity of intrinsic nature.
Fifth is ultimate impurity.
First, regarding the observation of the impurity of the place of birth:
it refers to the woman’s dwelling for ten months between the two internal organs, the mature and the immature, within the womb.
Second, impurity of the seed:
this refers to the appropriation of another’s semen and blood, which combine to form the seed.
Third, impurity of specific characteristics: [this refers to...].
The impurities of the body flow out from the nine apertures.
Fourth, regarding the impurity of intrinsic nature:
one contemplates the impurity of the body.
It is like a person with clear vision opening a granary and seeing the grains of rice and millet;
one observes that it is filled with the impurities of the thirty-six constituents.
This is the fifth, ultimate impurity.
If this body were to die, it would become bloated,
rot, and decay, with worms, pus, and blood exposed— truly loathsome and distressing. Thus,
one sees these five kinds of impurity, which destroy the perversion of perceiving the pure as pure.
This is called the application of mindfulness to the internal body.
Contemplating the external body and both the internal and external bodies is likewise.
Second, regarding the application of mindfulness to feelings: one contemplates that internally there are the six sense faculties and externally there are the six sense objects.
Due to the conjunction of the sense faculties and their objects, the six consciousnesses arise.
From the arising of the six consciousnesses, the three types of feeling arise:
painful feeling, pleasant feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
One contemplates painful feelings as having the characteristic of the suffering of suffering (*duḥkhaduḥkhatā*).
One contemplates pleasant feelings as having the characteristic of the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkhatā*).
One contemplates neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings as having the characteristic of the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāraduḥkhatā*).

If the three types of sensation arising from the mental faculty are all equally suffering, then one destroys the inversion of regarding them as pleasure; this is called the foundation of mindfulness of internal sensations.
The same applies to external sensations and internal-external sensations.
Third, the application of mindfulness of the mind:
one contemplates that this mental consciousness is conditioned and belongs to causes and conditions;
therefore, it is impermanent—previously non-existent, now existent, and subsequently non-existent.
Because it arises and ceases moment by moment and thought by thought, it is impermanent;
this very fact refutes the perversion of permanence and is called the internal application of mindfulness (adhyātma-smṛtyupasthāna).
The same applies to external mind and both internal and external mind.
Regarding the four foundations of mindfulness:
one contemplates that the two aggregates of perception and mental formations, being a combination of causes and conditions, lack any inherent nature.
Arising is only the arising of dharmas; ceasing is only the ceasing of dharmas.
There is no person, no self, no sentient being, and no life-span.
None of these sixteen views can be apprehended.
The destruction of the inversion of self is called the mindfulness of internal dharmas;
the same applies to external dharmas and internal-external dharmas.
This is as explained in the *Tattvasiddhi* and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
This is the initial gateway to the foundations of mindfulness of nature (*dharmasmṛtyupasthāna*).
Second, regarding the foundations of mindfulness of nature that shatter views:
this refers to contemplating the two views of self and extremes (*satkāyadṛṣṭi* and *antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) as defiled and indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) within the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*).
The self is either identical to the aggregates or distinct from the aggregates;
the self exists within the aggregates or the aggregates exist within the self.
Upon investigation, the self cannot be found.
Destroying the twenty kinds of satkāyadṛṣṭi is called noble practice.
Next, one separately contemplates the five aggregates according to the view of antagrāhadṛṣṭi.
That which is termed the application of mindfulness to the body of nature (dharmatākāya) is as follows:
This is precisely the nature of form (*rūpa*).
Whether form is coarse or subtle, it is entirely impure.
Coarse form refers to the human body and the world.
The subtlest form reaches its limit in the atom (*paramāṇu*).
If one perceives even a minute particle as having constant coarse or subtle form,
such perception entirely depends upon form.
If one perceives coarse and subtle forms as impermanent,
as both permanent and impermanent,
or as neither permanent nor impermanent.
This view entirely depends on form: if it is eternal, there is the view;
if it is impermanent, there is no view;
and so too with that which is both eternal and impermanent.
This is the view that things both exist and do not exist;
it is neither permanence nor impermanence;
it is precisely the view that things neither exist nor do not exist.
These four views all depend upon form;
that is, they are the four extreme views regarding the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).
If one does not know this to be the aggregate of form as viewed through extreme views, [one remains bound].
Giving rise to conceptual understanding, attachment, and frivolous proliferation,
contention arises from views, which in turn give rise to all afflictions and fetters;
furthermore, because of these fetters, one commits all manner of evil karma.
Or, due to the fetters (*saṃyojana*), various wholesome karmas may arise;
yet through the flow of these fetters and karma, one transmigrates through the three realms and twenty-five states of existence (*bhava*) in a cycle of birth and death that has no end.
Why is this called not knowing the characteristics of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) as it relates to the extreme views (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*)?
