there remain only seven births as humans or devas;
this is increased by one final moment.
This refers to entering the stage of the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*).
A question is asked:
"Are the stages of Heat (*uṣmagata*) and Summits (*mūrdhan*) not also capable of endurance (*kṣānti*)?"
Why is it not called "Endurance" (Kṣānti)?
The answer is:
if one discusses the four roots of goodness in general.
These are also called the four patiences (*kṣānti*); however, because they are patient with the dharmas and do not regress, they are specifically designated by the name "patience.
If one at the stage of "heat" (*uṣmagata*) encounters adverse conditions, they may regress, commit the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*), and slander the Vaipulya sūtras.
One who becomes an icchantika falls into the Avīci Hell; likewise,
one who regresses from the stage of the "summit" (mūrdhan) due to encountering adverse conditions,
although not having severed their roots of goodness, still commits the five heinous crimes (ānantarya).
Now, in this dharma of patience, wisdom is strong and delusion is weak;
thus, one cannot be moved by any evils,
for the power of patience is great.
All evil minds are non-analytical cessations (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha),
just as the various beasts keep their distance from the lion king. Question:
If one falls back from the stages of *uṣmagata* or *mūrdhan*,
how can they be called those of the *gotrabhū* stage?
The answer is:
Although this person has committed evil and fallen into hell,
once they have entered and completed their punishment, they shall never enter again.
Because they possess the roots of goodness of the "nature-ground" (gotrabhū), they are able to attain the fruit of the noble ones (ārya-phala).
Therefore, a sutra says:
"It would be better to be Devadatta than to be Udraka Rāmaputra; for although Devadatta committed the three heinous crimes and fell into hell,"
Born among humans, he attained the state of a Pratyekabuddha;
his faculties were more sharp and keen than those of Śāriputra.
Seventh, regarding the stage of the World-First Dharma (laukikāgradharma):
The most excellent roots of goodness attained by ordinary persons are called the Supreme Mundane Dharmas (*laukikāgradharma*).
They are also the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) that are wholesome yet subject to outflows (*sāsrava*).
It is also the nature of wisdom.
The highest patience (*adhimātrā kṣānti*) relies on the meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) of six stages for a single moment (*kṣaṇa*),
thereby giving rise to the most excellent root of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) for that one moment.
This is called the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*).
In this single moment, it is endowed with the five powers (*pañcabala*).
Regarding the four aspects of the Truth of Suffering, one aspect follows conditions for a single moment and does not abide.
Therefore, it resembles the Path of Seeing. Why is this?
Because there are two types of practitioners.
First, those whose conduct is dominated by craving; second, those whose conduct is dominated by views.
Conduct dominated by craving is of two kinds.
The conduct of pride increases; the conduct of indolence increases;
and the conduct of views is likewise of two kinds.

That is to say, regarding "self" and "what belongs to self," those who are attached to the conceit of "I" cultivate the practice of impermanence and enter the stage of the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*).
Those with increased indolence enter by practicing asceticism;
those attached to a self enter by practicing the non-self;
those attached to "mine" enter by practicing emptiness.
As he cultivates the stage of the total mindfulness of the body (*kāyagatāsati*), a mind of certainty arises in succession.
There are nine grades of mundane wholesome states;
the lowest-of-the-low, the middle-of-the-low, and the highest-of-the-low are called the "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) dharmas.
The middle-lower, middle-middle, and middle-upper are called the Dharma of the Summit (mūrdhan).
The upper-middle, upper-lower, and upper-middle are called the Dharma of Patience (kṣānti).
The upper-upper is called the Supreme Mundane Dharma (laukikāgradharma).
If one contemplates the five aggregates as impermanent and so forth, these roots of goodness are called the stage of "Heat" (ūṣmagata).
Contemplating the merits of the Triple Gem is called the stage of "Summit" (mūrdhan).
Contemplating the Noble Truths is called the stage of "Patience" (kṣānti).
The noble path that follows the contemplation of the noble truth of suffering is called the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgradharma*).
The stage of heat (*uṣmagata*) is abandoned either through falling away, through relinquishing, or at the end of life.
If one abandons them by crossing over realms or stages,
the same applies to the *mūrdhan* (Summits) stage.
For the *kṣānti* (Patience) stage, there is no abandonment through falling back.
The relinquishment of the remaining two is the same as above.
The Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) has no relinquishment because it lasts for only a single moment.
Furthermore, regarding these persons who possess the four roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*):
All of these employ the dharma-smṛtyupasthāna through the commonality of their intrinsic nature;
the path of cultivation is likewise another name for the four smṛtyupasthānas,
which are attained once and never lost.
This refers to the meaning of receiving a superior name.
Regarding the *vibhāṣā* (exegesis) on the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*),
there were ultimately dozens of different interpretations from various schools.
The names and meanings of the seven worthies are immeasurable;
how could they be known by ordinary people? Question:
The stages of the seven worthies progress from shallow to deep;
for what reason do you specifically explain only the stage of dry wisdom?
The stage of the nature of discernment is not detailed here.
The answer is:
the stage of dry wisdom is the shallowest.
As analyzed above,
it is already difficult for oneself to know and cannot be fathomed by the world;
it is precisely the point where the branches of the correct and the false diverge for those at the initial stage of practice.
All practitioners of the Buddha-dharma must briefly analyze the points in which those who study and those who practice meditation are deluded and submerged.
If one enters the Stage of Dry Wisdom, the eye of liberating insight arises;
this is beyond the measurement of ordinary beings.
How can the many words of those who speak falsely be trusted?
Therefore, when lecturing and reciting for a single household,
one must provide a detailed explanation from the perspective of the beginner's mind;
however, regarding the profound stages of the sages and saints, one need only provide a brief topical outline.
Those who practice seated meditation should briefly grasp the general meaning of the Buddha-dharma,
and must immediately awaken to impermanence, repent, and cultivate the Path.
How could one possibly pursue such urgentless talk?
If one wishes to proclaim that which benefits all beings,
one must clearly grasp this correct intent and its distinct names and characteristics.
If there are points not fully understood, one should seek them out further for oneself.
This concludes the brief exposition of the seven stages of the worthies.
End of Fascicle Five of the *Sìjiàoyì* (The Meaning of the Four Teachings).
The Meaning of the Four Teachings, Fascicle Six.
Composed by Master Zhiyi of Xiu Chan Temple on Mount Tiantai.

Second, explaining the seven stages of the noble ones (*ārya-pudgala*): first, those who follow through faith (*śraddhānusārin*); second, those who follow through the Dharma (*dharmānusārin*); third, those who possess faith...
The fourth is the one who attains through vision;
the fifth is the one who realizes through the body.
The Arhat of six-fold liberation and the Arhat of non-timely liberation;
these seven classes are collectively termed "Noble Ones" (ārya).
To take correctness as the meaning is precisely to polish the Way and suspend the mirror;
through the patience of suffering and true illumination, one abandons the nature of an ordinary person.
One attains entry into the nature of the noble ones (*ārya*).
Because true wisdom perceives the principle and severs the obstacles of the homogeneous class (*sabhāga-pratighāta*),
one is therefore called "noble."
These seven noble persons (āryapudgala) further differ in two ways:
namely, those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
The first five types of noble persons are all individuals in training.
The latter two types of noble persons belong to the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).
As for those called "persons in training" (*śaikṣa*),
they begin from the moment they attain true wisdom through the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*).
From that time onward, there were finally noble ones (ārya).
There are two kinds of five aggregates (pañca-skandha): those with outflows (sāsrava) and those without outflows (anāsrava).
Because they perceive the traces of the noble ones, they are called learners (śaikṣa).
Because they no longer seek or investigate the truths, they are called those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
Furthermore, as for those beyond training,
their true wisdom has reached the ultimate limit regarding the principles of the three realms.
Even if [the afflictions] have already been exhausted such that there are no delusions remaining to be treated,
it is not necessary to further study the four noble truths;
one simply proceeds to the stage of the seven types of noble beings.
It is divided into three paths:
namely, the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), and the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*).
First, regarding the path of seeing:
This is precisely the Eightfold Noble Path.
By seeing the principle, one severs the delusions of the truths;
this continues until the fifteenth moment of mind.
It is like the method of breaking a stone.
Second, regarding the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*),
this refers to the contemplation that eliminates [afflictions] by means of observing each of the truths through the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*).
The skillful means for severing it is like cutting the fibers from the root of a lotus.
As for the three paths of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*),
they are to be distinguished as previously explained.
First, regarding the stage of the follower by faith (*śraddhānusārin*):
this is the designation for a person of dull faculties who enters the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).
As for what is meant by "dull faculties," it refers to being dull because one relies on the understanding generated through others rather than through the cultivation of one's own wisdom.
This person is on the path of skillful means;
although they previously possessed faith, because they have not yet given rise to the truth, it is not called "practice.
Practice takes the sense of advancing and progressing as its definition.

From the moment one attains the true illumination of the patience regarding suffering (*duḥkha-kṣānti*) for fifteen moments, one progresses toward the vision of reality and is termed a "follower by faith" (*śraddhānusārin*).
Therefore, it is said that there are only those who practice in proximity; there are no practitioners who have traveled far.
Furthermore, it is impossible for one to pass away while in any of the fifteen moments of mind;
such would be the case regarding the patience toward the dharma of suffering (duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti).
The antidote to the ten proclivities abandoned through vision in the desire realm is this dharma;
it is the first untainted path of non-obstruction (*anantarya-mārga*).
Furthermore, there is the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgra-dharma*).
In succession, one does not act, does not incline toward, and does not proceed;
having thus been able to abandon wrong actions, wrong destinies, and wrong views,
one further distinguishes the patience regarding the dharma of suffering (*duḥkha-dharma-kṣānti*), which is the supreme mundane dharma (*laukikāgra-dharma*).
Five kinds of determination are established:
namely, determination of the stage, determination of the mode of activity, determination of the object, determination of the moment, and determination of the sequential condition.
Regarding the determination of the sequential condition:
Immediately after the Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*), one enters the Receptivity to Suffering (*duḥkhakṣānti*).
As the *Abhidharmahṛdaya-śāstra* verse states:
"The same applies to form and formless realms, as well as to suffering, origin, cessation, and the path."
This dharma of immediate realization is explained as the sixteen moments of mind.
Fifteen moments of mind constitute the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*),
while the sixteenth moment belongs to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
If you argue that this should not be the case,
then just as the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna) is accomplished,
it too should belong to the path of no-more-learning (aśaikṣamārga).
This practitioner of faith (śraddhānusārin), during the fifteen moments of mind on the path of seeing,
is also called one on the stage of the "eight persons" (aṣṭamaka-bhūmi).
They possess eight of the patiences (kṣānti) and are deficient by only one part of the knowledges (jñāna).
This is the stage of the candidate for the fruit of stream-entry (srotāpattipratipannaka);
"candidate" is also termed the stream-enterer in the midst of practice.
Second, the clarification of the stage of one who practices in accordance with the Dharma (dharmānusārī).
This is the name for those of sharp faculties entering the Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*).
As for "those of sharp faculties," it refers to those who,
by means of their own wisdom, permeate their vision of the principle and sever the fetters.
Therefore, it is called "benefit" (li).
It originally resides within the path of skillful means,
wherein one is able to employ the wisdom of contemplation to observe the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths.
However, as long as true insight has not yet arisen, it cannot be called "practice.
Through the World’s Supreme Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*), one gives rise to the true illumination of the Patience regarding Suffering (*duḥkha-kṣānti*).
In fifteen moments, one progresses toward the vision of the truth.
Therefore, it is called "Dharma-practice" (dharmacaryā).
The classification of the categories of Dharma-practice is similar to that of the preceding "Faith-practice" (śraddhācaryā);
the explanation can be understood accordingly.
The only difference is that those of dull faculties rely on others to produce understanding and have little analytical observation through their own wisdom,
whereas those of sharp faculties have much analytical observation through their own wisdom.
This refers to the stage of liberation through faith (*śraddhādhimukta*).

This refers to the person who practices through faith (*śraddhā-carita*). Upon entering the path of cultivation (*bhāvanā-mārga*), they are renamed a person of resolute understanding (*adhimukti-jña*).
Having dull faculties, they rely upon others to give rise to true understanding through faith.
Therefore, it is called "resolute belief" (adhimukti).
There are three ways in which such a person of resolute belief realizes the fruits:
first, they realize the fruit of a stream-enterer (srotāpanna-phala).
Second, those who realize the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin*;
third, those who realize the fruit of *anāgāmin*.
First, regarding those who clearly understand and realize the fruit of *srotāpanna*:
The sixteenth path is associated with subsequent knowledge (*anvaya-jñāna*),
which is the realization of the fruit of *srotāpanna*.
*Srotāpanna* is a term from the land of India.
This translates as "cultivating the untainted" (*anāsrava*).
According to the *Abhidharmakośa*, this still refers to the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*);
according to the meaning explained by the Sautrāntikas, it refers to the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
Upon realizing the fruit, one enters the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
This provides a convenient way to explain, in a single stroke, the meaning of cultivating the untainted (*anāsrava*).
As for what is abandoned by vision (*darśana-prahātavya*), it is briefly stated as the exhaustion of the three fetters (*saṃyojana*).
To explain in detail: one who has exhausted the eighty-eight latent proclivities (anuśaya) is called a srotāpanna;
having undergone birth and death seven times at most, they will never undergo an eighth birth.
Second, those of clear understanding and conviction realize the fruit of sakṛdāgāmin.
There are two kinds:
the one-directional and the two-fruit.
The one-directional occurs from after the mind of the first fruit.
Furthermore, by practicing the contemplation of the sixteen truths,
the seven factors of enlightenment manifest before one;
thus, in this very life, one eliminates a category of afflictions through the outflow-free path.
When one uses the path of non-obstruction to sever one or two grades of afflictions of the desire realm,
or uses the path of non-obstruction to sever up to five grades,
all such individuals are candidates for the fruit of once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin).
They are also called "superior Srotāpannas.
It is with reference to these that the "family-to-family" (kulaṃkula) practitioner is described.
Regarding the second fruit: if one has completely severed six grades [of afflictions], [one is a Sakṛdāgāmin].
To realize the liberation of the sixth grade of the desire realm is precisely the fruit of the Sakṛdāgāmin.
"Sakṛdāgāmin" is a term from the language of India.
This is translated as "thin.
The afflictions of the desire realm are divided into nine grades;
six grades have been exhausted, while three grades remain.
Because that which has already been severed is much,
while that which remains unsevered is little,
it is called "thin."
Those who possess the three types of clear understanding and realization and have attained the stage of *anāgāmin* are also of two kinds:
those who are exclusively directed toward the second fruit and those who are directed toward the third.
Regarding "one who is exclusively [on the path]": if one has abandoned seven or even eight grades of the desire realm,
they are all candidates for the stage of non-returner (*anāgāmin-patipannaka*),
and are also called "superior progressors" (*viśeṣa-gāmin*) toward the stage of once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*).
Based on this, one type of seed is explained.
Second, regarding the clarification of the fruit:
through the nine unimpeded paths, one abandons the fetters of the desire realm.
Realizing the ninth liberation is precisely what is called the fruit of *anāgāmin*.
*Anāgāmin* is a term from the land of India.
This is translated as "Non-returner" (Anāgāmin).
This person has exhausted the five lower fetters (pañca avara-bhāgīya-saṃyojanāni) of the desire realm and will no longer be reborn there.
Therefore, it is said that he does not return.
Furthermore, there are three types of *srotāpanna*:
first, the *srotāpanna* within the course of practice (*pratipannaka*).
This refers to the candidate for the fruit of stream-entry (*srotāpatti-pratipannaka*).
Second, abiding in the fruit is precisely the fruit of stream-entry itself (*srotāpanna-phala*).
Third, superior progress refers to the further advancement of the stream-enterer.
This is also called "family-to-family" (kulaṃkula),
which refers to the stage of one heading toward the fruit of once-returner (sakṛdāgāmin).
There are only two types of once-returners.
First, abiding in the fruit;
second, advancing.
The one who advances toward the fruit of sakṛdāgāmin is also called "one-seeded."
This is the stage of one progressing toward the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmī-pratipannaka).
There are also two types of non-returners:
first, those who abide in the fruit.
Second is superior progress.
One who has progressed to the stage of a non-returner (anāgāmin) further severs the five higher fetters.
The so-called fetters of attachment to the realm of form and attachment to the formless realm, and so forth, refer to those who are candidates for arhatship (arhattvaphalapratipannaka).
As for the arhat, they abide solely in the fruit. A question was asked: [What is the distinction between the candidate and the one abiding in the fruit?]
This explains attaining the fruits through successive stages.
The Abhidharma clarifies attaining the fruits by means of transcendence (*vyutkrāntaka*).
How are these distinguished?
The answer is: If,
while still an ordinary person (pṛthagjana),
one has severed from six to eight grades of the fetters (saṃyojana) of the desire realm (kāmadhātu).
Before entering the path of seeing the truths,
one subsequently gives rise to the true illumination of the patience regarding suffering (*duḥkha-kṣānti*);
during these fifteen moments of mind, one is a candidate for the stage of once-returner (*sakṛdāgāmin*).
The sixteen moments of mind constitute the realization of the fruit of Sakṛdāgāmin.

If, during the stage of an ordinary person (pṛthagjana), one has first severed the ninth grade of the desire realm up to the sphere of nothingness, and subsequently enters the fifteen moments of mind of the path of seeing (darśanamārga).
This is called the stage of "one heading toward non-returning" (anāgāmipratipannaka).
At the sixteenth moment of mind, one realizes the fruit of non-returning.
This refers to a person of "leap-over" attainment who does not realize the two preceding fruits; although this is a person of faith-understanding (śraddhādhimukta), they are of dull faculties.
There are five types of spiritual faculties (indriya) that differ, namely:
those subject to regression, those who attain through reflection, those who guard their attainment, those who abide in their state, and those who progress toward excellence.
This applies when one realizes the fruit of anāgāmin.
Furthermore, there are five kinds of parinirvāṇa, seven kinds of parinirvāṇa, and eight kinds of parinirvāṇa.
Regarding the five kinds of parinirvāṇa:
first is intermediate parinirvāṇa (antarāparinirvāṇa).
2. One who attains parinirvāṇa after being reborn (upapadyaparinirvāyin). 3. One who attains parinirvāṇa through exertion (sābhisamskāraparinirvāyin).
4. One who attains parinirvāṇa without exertion (anabhisamskāraparinirvāyin).
The fifth is the one who attains parinirvāṇa in the upper stream (*ūrdhvasrotas*).
Regarding the seven types of those who attain parinirvāṇa,
the one who attains parinirvāṇa in the intermediate state (*antarāparinirvāyin*) is divided into three kinds.
Regarding the eight types of parinirvāṇa:
five are as previously described;
[the remaining three] are parinirvāṇa with full accomplishment, parinirvāṇa in the formless realm, and parinirvāṇa without fixed timing.
Regarding "the four clarities of attaining the subsequent stages":
for one who practices according to the Dharma (dharmānusārin), the transition into the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga) is termed "attaining through vision" (darśana-prāpti).
These are persons of sharp faculties who,
by means of their own wisdom, cultivate insight and attain the principle upon seeing the Dharma; therefore,
they are called "attainers through vision" (dṛṣṭiprāpta).
This refers to seeing that a person, while on the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga),
sequentially realizes the three fruits or transcends them to realize two fruits.
This is also as distinguished in the section on faith and understanding;
however, because their faculties are sharp,
they do not rely upon hearing the Dharma nor require the full assembly of external conditions.
The distinction lies in being able to personally see the Dharma and realize its principle.
Seeing that one possesses sharp faculties,
it is simply the nature of the immovable faculty.
If one realizes the fruit of *anāgāmin*,
there are likewise five types of *parinirvāṇa* as well as seven and eight different types.
Regarding the fifth, the stage of bodily realization (*kāyasākṣin*):
Alternatively, those who possess faith-understanding and insight enter the path of cultivation and,
by means of untainted wisdom, sever the five lower fetters.
Due to the five higher fetters (*pañca-ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana*), one gives rise to the four dhyānas and the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*).

One then employs the common foundations of mindfulness (*sāmānya-smṛtyupasthāna*) to cultivate the eight liberations (*aṣṭa-vimokṣa*), the eight bases of mastery (*aṣṭa-abhibhvāyatana*), the ten totalities (*daśa-kṛtsnāyatana*), and the entry into the nine successive attainments (*navānupūrva-samāpatti*) as well as the three doors of liberation (*trīṇi vimokṣamukhāni*).
Having already completely severed the two obstacles of nature,
and further severing the obstacle of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, one attains the principle that conditions for cessation are extinguished;
thus, all minds and mental factors enter the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*).
Because he has attained this meditative absorption, he is called an "Anāgāmin who has realized through the body" (kāyasākṣin). Why is this?
Because entering the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) resembles the dharma of nirvāṇa.
By settling within the body, one brings to rest all the labors of the three realms;
having personally realized the cessation of perception and feeling,
it is therefore called "bodily realization" (*kāyasākṣin*).
If one explains the "body-witness" (kāyasākṣin) in relation to the first fruit [of stream-entry],
it is simply because they previously, while still an ordinary person (pṛthagjana),
used conventional knowledge (saṃvṛtijñāna) to sever the fetters.
Having attained the four dhyānas and the four formless absorptions,
he subsequently attains the sixteenth moment of mind upon seeing the truths and realizes the fruit of non-returning (anāgāmin).
He then cultivates the applications of mindfulness associated with the mundane.

Returning from the desire realm, one cultivates the liberations (*vimokṣa*), the bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*), the spheres of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*), and enters the nine successive attainments (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*).
Thus, one achieves the realization of the body (*kāyasākṣin*).
There are two types of non-returners (*anāgāmin*).
The first is one who abides in the fruit, who is simply an Anāgāmin.
The second is one who, while still possessing the fruit, practices toward the next stage;
this is the Anāgāmin of superior progress.
Because they are still designated as those "practicing toward the stage of Anāgāmin," they are subsumed under the category of those "practicing toward Arhatship" (Arhattva-pratipannaka). Thus,
the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
That [category] contains eleven types.
Five types of *anāgāmin* are precisely *anāgāmin*;
six types of *anāgāmin* are subsumed under the stage of the candidate for *arhatship* (*arhattvaphalapratipannaka*).
It should be known that this body realizes the stage of *anāgāmin*;
this is precisely the superior advancement of the *anāgāmin*,
which is subsumed under the path of the candidate for *arhat* (*arhattvaphalapratipannaka*).
The five types of *anāgāmin* and the seven types of *anāgāmin* all consist exclusively of those who attain parinirvāṇa by ascending (*ūrdhvasrotas*).

The eight types of *anāgāmin* consist only of those who attain parinirvāṇa in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharma-parinirvāyin*) and those who attain parinirvāṇa in the formless realm (*ārūpya-parinirvāyin*).
Such is the Abhidharma, categorized according to those who attain through faith-understanding (*śraddhādhimukta*) and those who attain through vision (*dṛṣṭiprāpta*).
If one were to enumerate them by category,
there would be twelve thousand nine hundred and sixty types of *anāgāmin*.
To explain such great matters in detail, how could one possibly trouble oneself with such detailed classification?
Sixth, regarding the Arhat liberated by time (samaya-vimukta):
this refers to one who follows through faith (śraddhānusārin) and possesses dull faculties;
they attain liberation only after waiting for the proper time and the assembly of various conditions.
Therefore, they are called "liberated by time" (samayavimukta).
The term "arhat" is an Indian word.
This term has no equivalent translation in this land [of China] and encompasses three meanings.
First, "slayer of thieves" (arhat).
Second, non-arising;
third, being worthy of offerings.
Possessing these three meanings, one abides in the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*).
There are five types of arhats;
that is to say, five types arise from those who follow by faith (śraddhānusārin):

and who aspire to seek the supreme Dharma, one should preach the Pratyekabuddha vehicle for them;
these are all those whose causes and conditions lead to awakening as a Pratyekabuddha.
The three types and ten categories of root-natures (indriya) can be understood as resulting from differences in past conditions (*pūrvapratyaya*). Regarding the fourth point,
the method of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*):
There are two types of contemplation on the twelve links of dependent origination:
first, the contemplation of the twelve links of dependent origination belonging to craving;
second, the contemplation of the twelve links of dependent origination belonging to views.
Regarding the first contemplation on the twelve links of dependent origination as belonging to craving,
there are two intentions:
first, investigation.
Second, refutation through contemplation.
First, as for the seeker:
this person hears the teaching on phenomena arising and ceasing through correct causes and conditions.
With clear faith and understanding, one awakens to all things;
those belonging to craving and affliction are entirely the twelve links of dependent origination.
He entered meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Desiring to still the mind and reach the fundamental source, he sought natural wisdom (*svayambhū-jñāna*).
Delighting in solitary tranquility, he cultivated the practice of stabilizing the mind and attained various dhyāna concentrations.
Abiding in this meditative concentration, one knows that the afflictions associated with craving are none other than ignorance.
By investigating them in both reverse and forward order, one perceives the twelve links of dependent origination.
How does one investigate them in reverse? From what cause does this craving arise?
One then knows that feeling is caused by contact.
One further knows that feeling arises because of what? It arises because of contact.
Thus, one asks: from what does contact arise?
That is, the six sense bases are conditioned by [the five aggregates]; the six sense bases are conditioned by name-and-form;
name-and-form is conditioned by consciousness.
Consciousness has its cause in volitional formations (*saṃskāra*);
volitional formations have their cause in ignorance (*avidyā*), which refers to all afflictions (*kleśa*) of the past.
Furthermore, one should trace back this craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
Craving can give rise to grasping;
conditioned by grasping, the karma of existence is formed.
Because of this karma of existence, there is birth within the twenty-five realms of existence in the future.
From these causes arise old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, and a mass of suffering;
thus one revolves through the cycle without end.
However, if one stabilizes the mind through contemplation and enters deep meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), [the cycle is brought to an end].
Investigating by tracing back in this manner,
one may at times see the *kalala* stage of initial conception,
and even see the past body giving rise to karma and afflictions.
This continues up to two births, a hundred thousand births,
or even more; one follows the search and grasps at existence through the power of meditative concentration.
Or they may see one future life, up to ten, a hundred, or a thousand lives.
If they see events of the past or the future,
their hearts are moved with compassion, and their resolve for the path becomes vigorous and diligent.
It increases and becomes even more intense.

Second, clarifying the contemplation that breaks through the twelve links of dependent origination belonging to craving is precisely the *dharmasmṛtyupasthāna* (foundation of mindfulness on phenomena).
This is the sequential contemplation of the twelve links of dependent origination.
The contemplation of the foundations of mindfulness regarding their intrinsic nature is roughly as previously explained. Why is this so?
If one contemplates craving as being the nature of the five aggregates of defilement, this is the four foundations of mindfulness.
If one contemplates feeling, contact, the six sense bases, name-and-form, and consciousness,
this is the four foundations of mindfulness as the nature of the five indeterminate aggregates that constitute present retribution.
If one contemplates formations,
this is the four foundations of mindfulness regarding the nature of the five aggregates as wholesome or unwholesome.
If one contemplates ignorance...
This is the four foundations of mindfulness regarding the nature of the five aggregates of past defiled afflictions.
If one contemplates grasping,
this is the four foundations of mindfulness regarding the nature of the present defiled five aggregates.
If one contemplates existence,
this refers to the four foundations of mindfulness regarding the nature of the five aggregates— both wholesome and unwholesome— in the present;
if one contemplates future birth, aging, and death, it refers to the same.
This refers to the four foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) that arise as a result of karmic retribution and are of an indeterminate nature (avyākṛta).
By employing these four foundations of mindfulness,
one contemplates the twelve links of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) both in direct and reverse order to destroy the four inversions (viparyāsa).
If inversion is extinguished, that is the extinction of ignorance and all afflictions.
Because ignorance is extinguished, volitional formations are extinguished,
and so on until old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair are extinguished.
This is called the four foundations of mindfulness in terms of their functional nature;
it is the wisdom of contemplation that sequentially observes the twelve links of dependent origination as belonging to the afflictions of craving.
Second, the explanation of the contemplation that destroys the twelve links of dependent origination as belonging to the afflictions of views.
This also has two purposes:
first, investigative inquiry;
second, contemplative refutation.
First, as for those who investigate and seek:
if they perceive the self and the world as eternal,
or as both eternal and non-eternal.
"Neither eternal nor non-eternal"—
this constitutes the four views regarding the present existence and the self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
Based on these four views regarding the present existence and the self, [the following arises].
The fourteen difficult questions and the sixty-two views arise from these;
the four views regarding the self and the extremes are themselves the four graspings.
One investigates these four graspings both in their direct and reverse orders.
Tracing back, the four graspings arise from the four cravings;
the four cravings arise from the four feelings.
The four feelings have the four contacts as their cause;
the four contacts have the four bases as their cause;
the four bases have name-and-form as their cause.
The fourfold name-and-form has the fourfold consciousness as its cause;
the fourfold consciousness has the fourfold formations as its cause;
and the fourfold formations have the fourfold types of ignorance as their cause.
Furthermore, following the four types of seeking (*paryeṣaṇā*) and the four types of grasping (*upādāna*), these give rise to the four kinds of existence (*bhava*).
These four existences encompass all twenty-five modes of birth, as well as aging, illness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction.
If, by means of stabilizing the mind through contemplation,
one attains deep meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) and perceives events of past or future lives,
it is exactly as previously described.
Second, the explanation of the contemplation that breaks [delusion]:
the contemplation of the four foundations of mindfulness according to their causal nature contemplates the four graspings and the four views regarding self and body.
In this sequence, continuing down to ignorance,
one refutes [the views] that there was a past going forth, not going forth,
both going forth and not going forth, and neither going forth nor not going forth.
It is neither that which has gone nor that which has not gone.
The two views of self-identity and extremes defile the five aggregates.
Furthermore, there are four graspings to be observed accordingly.
Even unto future birth and death,
one shatters the views of finitude, infinitude,
both finitude and infinitude, and neither finitude nor infinitude.
It is neither finite nor infinite.
The two views of self-existence and extremes defile the five aggregates.
If one can thus employ the four foundations of mindfulness according to their true nature, [the defilements will be eliminated].
By destroying the four views— the two views of self-existence and self-annihilation regarding the three periods of time—
one simultaneously eradicates all afflictions associated with views, including the fourteen difficult questions and the sixty-two views.
This is called: with the cessation of ignorance, formations cease;
and so on, up to the cessation of old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair.
If it pertains to the cessation of afflictions associated with views.
Thereupon, one again employs the aforementioned contemplation on the nature of the twelve links of dependent origination through the four foundations of mindfulness;
by this, craving for the realm of desire, the realm of form, and the formless realm are all destroyed and extinguished.
This is the extinction of the afflictions, karma, and paths of action within the three realms.
This is called nirvana with remainder.
If one extinguishes the path of craving and suffering,
this is nirvana without remainder.
This is called the wisdom of the four foundations of mindfulness in their functional nature (*yongsu shes pa'i rang bzhin*).
By contemplating the twelve links of dependent origination, one enters nirvana.
The contemplation of the foundations of mindfulness in their essential nature (*rang bzhin gyi dran pa nye bar bzhag pa*) is briefly as explained previously.
Therefore, a sutra states:
"The meaning of the twelve links of dependent origination is extremely profound;
it is difficult to understand and difficult to perceive. This is precisely what is intended here.
When the Buddha was preaching the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra,
there was a non-Buddhist practitioner named Pūraṇa who questioned the World-Honored One, saying:
"Gautama, how do you lead me to understand that the self and the world are eternal... [and so on] ...up to being neither eternal nor non-eternal?
The Buddha replied:
If you can exhaust what is old and not create what is new,
then you will be able to know that the self and the world are eternal,
up to and including being neither eternal nor non-eternal.
The brahmin immediately said,
"I have already understood.
The Buddha asked:
"How do you know this?
The brahmin replied,
"Therefore it is called ignorance."
If one knows that there is grasping for existence (*upādāna-bhava*), yet understands that ignorance (*avidyā*) does not arise,
then one knows that the self (*ātman*) and the world are eternal.
...up to "neither eternal nor non-eternal.
At that time, the brahmin sought to go forth as a disciple of the Buddha.

Furthermore, the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* clarifies that the Śrāvaka sūtras enter the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*) by means of contemplating the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅgapratītyasamutpāda*).
One destroys the sixty-two views to enter the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
If one deeply realizes this intent,
it does not stop at merely refuting externalists.
If a disciple of the Buddha studies, engages in inquiry, or practices seated meditation,
yet gives rise to various views, becomes attached to them, and engages in contentious debate,
they will give rise to all manner of afflictions and the karma for birth and death within the twenty-five realms of existence.
All of these belong to the contemplation of the twelve links of dependent origination.
One who awakens to and understands this can employ the application of mindfulness to the nature of phenomena.
Upon investigation and penetration, one can attain liberation;
those who are deluded regarding this cycle through the twelve links of dependent origination wander in birth and death without end.
Therefore, the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states:
"The true Dharma, its expounder,
and its listener are difficult to find."
Therefore, in this way, birth and death are neither finite nor infinite.
This is the application of mindfulness through shared mindfulness;
it assists in the contemplation of the twelve links of dependent origination.
The preceding cases may be understood by analogy.
Regarding the fivefold classification and analysis:
a question is asked:
If one asks: "If awakening occurs naturally through past habitual practice, why is it necessary for the Buddha to teach the twelve links of dependent origination?
The answer is:
If one explains it, one will attain it quickly;
if one does not explain it, awakening on one's own is somewhat delayed.
It is like a ripe fruit which, though it ought to fall by itself, [does so sooner if shaken].
If one wishes to take it quickly, it will fall by merely shaking it slightly.
[The interlocutor] asked:
"What of the Pratyekabuddhayāna?"
For what reason is the fruit not determined?
The answer is:
because śrāvakas are of dull faculties, their fruit is determined.
If a pratyekabuddha has long practiced wisdom and possesses sharp spiritual faculties,
there is no need to determine his stage of fruition.
It is, for example, like two people traveling together.
Those whose bodies are weak must stop to rest;
those whose bodies are strong proceed directly to their destination.
Therefore, the Buddha spoke only of the path of the pratyekabuddha.
The stage of fruition is not established.
Furthermore, because the general perception severs the fetters through coarse wisdom,
it removes only the active outbursts (*paryavasthāna*).
This is called the Śrāvaka-yāna.
By contemplating causes and conditions with a distinct conceptualization,
their wisdom is so subtle that it eradicates even the latent predispositions (*vāsanā*).
They are called Pratyekabuddhas.
Furthermore, because Śrāvakas are of duller faculties,
they first contemplate the Truth of Suffering.
Because the Pratyekabuddhas possess sharp faculties, they first contemplate the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*).
Question: Regarding the applications of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) of the Śrāvakas...
One might think that the specific perception is coarse and the general perception is superior;
why then is it now said that the general perception is coarse and the specific perception is superior?
Answer: It is because one again employs both specific and general perceptions to conduct a detailed, sequential contemplation of the twelve links of dependent origination;
therefore, the specific [contemplation] is superior.

Furthermore, the power of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) of the śrāvaka’s merit is shallow, and his divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) reaches only as far as a small thousandfold world system (*sāhasracūḍikalokadhātu*).
The pratyekabuddha, having long planted roots of goodness, possesses deep power of meditative concentration.
If one develops the divine eye, it surpasses three thousand [worlds] and perceives other world-systems.
This concludes the brief explanation of the stage of the Pratyekabuddha according to the "Gate of Existence" within the Tripiṭaka Teaching.
The Gate of Emptiness is like the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*.
The *Vibhāṣā* (Pifen Kunle) is a gate that is neither empty nor existent.
Since these scriptures and treatises have not yet been transmitted here, they cannot be known.

Compiled by Master Zhiyi of Xiu Chan Temple on Mount Tiantai.
Third, regarding the explanation of the meaning of "Pure Vimalakīrti" by clarifying the bodhisattva stages according to the Tripiṭaka teaching:
the Tripiṭaka teaching elucidates the principle of the arising and ceasing of dependent origination.
The meaning of the Bodhisattva-piṭaka should likewise possess four gates; here,
we shall treat it according to the "Gate of Existence" (astivāda) from the Abhidharma.
This clarifies the stages of a Mahāyāna Bodhisattva,
which consists of four points.
The first is the translation.
Second, the analysis of the stages;
third, the critical examination;
fourth, the explanation of the meaning of "Vimalakīrti."
First Translation:
That which is called "bodhisattva-mahāsattva" is a term from the language of India.
If one were to follow that terminology precisely,
it should be stated as *bodhisattva mahāsattva*; however,
the various masters differ in their translations.
I shall not detail it here;
however, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Dazhidu lun) translates it as:
"Bodhi is called the Buddha-way."
"Sattva" means "to accomplish sentient beings.
"Mahā" means "great.
This person accomplishes sentient beings by means of the Great Way of all Buddhas.
Furthermore, there is a master who translates it as follows:
"Bodhi" means the Way (Dharma),
and "sattva" means mind (citta).
"Mahā" means "Great Path"; thus, it refers to the path-mind and the great path-mind.
As for why various sutras and treatises frequently refer to them as "Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas," Master Kumārajīva [noted] that the Indic language was prolix.
The two lines consist of eight characters that serve as the title;
therefore, three characters are removed and five characters are retained to form a single sentence.
They are called Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas.
While the enlightenment of all three vehicles is collectively termed the "Path," the Bodhisattva alone receives this great title.
Because they give rise to the four great vows of compassion based on the Four Noble Truths—
seeking the fruit of Buddhahood above and transforming sentient beings below—
and because this mind is so vast and great, they are specifically designated by the title *mahāsattva*.
Second, the analysis of the bodhisattva stage consists briefly of seven points.
The first is the arousal of the bodhicitta.
Second, practicing the bodhisattva path;
third, the karma for the thirty-two marks;
fourth, the fulfillment of the six perfections.
Fifth, those in their final birth before Buddhahood;
sixth, those born in Tuṣita Heaven;
seventh and eighth, those who manifest the marks of perfection and attain enlightenment.
Regarding those who have once resolved their minds on bodhicitta:
for example, the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni was a potter in a past life.
He encountered Śākyamuni Buddha and made offerings to that Buddha;
furthermore, he saw that Buddha’s foremost disciple in wisdom,
named Śāriputra.
The disciple foremost in supernatural powers was named Maudgalyāyana;
the attendant renowned for his great learning was named Ānanda.
At that time, having made offerings to the Buddha,
the potter immediately gave rise to the bodhicitta and made this vow:
"I vow that in a future age I shall attain Buddhahood,
being called Śākyamuni once again,
and that my wise disciple shall be named Śāriputra."
The disciple foremost in spiritual power was named Maudgalyāyana;
the attendant foremost in learning was named Ānanda,
who could fulfill their wishes.
From this point, the initial arousal of the bodhicitta is precisely the arousal of the four great vows of compassion; however,
these are the four great vows of compassion according to the Tripiṭaka Teaching.
All arise based on the four truths of arising and ceasing.
As for what is called the mind of compassion, it consists first of the great heart of loving-kindness (*mahāmaitrī*).
The first is the joy of extinguishing the paths of the two types of sentient beings— those driven by desire and those driven by views.
The second is the great compassionate mind that seeks to uproot the suffering of the origin of suffering for these same two types of sentient beings.
Regarding the Four Great Vows:
the first is "to cause those not yet crossed over to cross over," which refers to the two types of attachment—
those of celestial demons and externalists, and those of craving and views.
First, regarding those sentient beings of the six realms who have not yet crossed over the suffering of the burning house of the triple world,
he causes them to attain deliverance.
Second, regarding those who have not yet attained understanding, he causes them to understand.
This refers to sentient beings of two types— those characterized by craving and those characterized by views—
who have not yet understood the karma of the twenty-five states of existence arising from craving and views;
[the teaching] gathers them so that they may attain understanding.
"Third, causing those who are not yet at peace to find peace" refers to sentient beings of two types— those driven by craving and those driven by views—
who have not yet found peace in the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment and all paths; it means causing them to find peace in the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*).
Fourth, causing those who have not yet attained nirvana to attain it:
these two types of sentient beings— those driven by craving and those driven by views—
have not yet extinguished the causes and effects of birth and death within the twenty-five realms of existence.
This is to cause all to attain the extinction of suffering, which is nirvana.
If one gives rise to the four great vows of compassion based on the four truths of arising and ceasing for the sake of sentient beings who are bound by the two types of craving and views, [then...]
This is precisely the Bodhisattva’s initial arousal of the bodhicitta.
Because they know the Four Noble Truths through the lens of attachment and views,
their wisdom surpasses that of all devas, māras, and non-Buddhists.
Because he possesses the merit of compassionate vows, he surpasses all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;
thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"From the first production of the thought of enlightenment, he becomes a teacher of gods and humans."
It surpasses all śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
As for the two types of bodhisattva practice,
these refer to practicing the six pāramitās throughout three asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
From the time of the past Śākyamuni Buddha until the time of Kanakamuni Buddha,
this period is called one asaṃkhyeya kalpa.
From then on, he was constantly free from a female body.
At that time, one does not know for oneself whether one will become a Buddha or not.
This constitutes the first asaṃkhyeya-kalpa,
which is precisely the stage of obtaining the five stabilizing minds (*pañca-sthāpana-citta*) and the mindfulness of individual and collective characteristics (*saṃjñā-vastu*).
One practices the six perfections through the application of mindfulness to objects, the application of mindfulness to concomitants, and the application of mindfulness to conditions.
The meaning of these three types of application of mindfulness is briefly as explained previously.
Why is this? Cultivating the *smṛtyupasthāna* of nature is for the purpose of destroying the demonic activities associated with craving;
it shatters all views associated with the six teachers who cultivate the *smṛtyupasthāna* shared with worldly beings.

Desiring to destroy the fetter of craving and shatter the supernatural powers of the six teachers, he practiced the foundations of mindfulness and preached the Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings bound by craving and views.
Because he severed the attachment to craving, the entire host of celestial Māras and their retinues was destroyed.
Because attachment and views have been destroyed, the three, six, and eighteen kinds of the Six Teachers,
as well as all the followers of external paths, are defeated. Therefore,
one employs the three bases of mindfulness to practice the six pāramitās.
Desiring to subdue the celestial Māras and to restrain the various non-Buddhist teachers,
when a Bodhisattva practices the six perfections by means of the three applications of mindfulness,
although they cultivate the applications of mindfulness regarding the nature of things, they do not sever the fetters.
In order to give birth within the three realms and deliver sentient beings,

one constantly desires to extensively cultivate the contemplation of the common foundations of mindfulness (*sādhāraṇasmṛtyupasthāna*) in order to attain supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and accomplish the fourth of the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), namely, acting in concert with others (*samānārthatā*).
They subdue sentient beings who are attached to views;

furthermore, they constantly and extensively cultivate the contemplation of the foundations of mindfulness in order to achieve the four analytical knowledges for preaching the Dharma of the Three Vehicles.
He transforms all sentient beings who cling to craving and views,
leading them together out of the burning house of the triple world.
This constitutes his practice of the six pāramitās during the first asaṃkhyeya kalpa.
By employing the Four Great Vows, one pacifies the mind of birth and death so that it is free from cowardice;
thus, even if the roots are impaired, one abandons the karma of a woman and constantly receives a male body.
At that time, one has not yet generated the stage of "Heat" (ūṣmagata) and remains among the external ordinary beings (bāhyapṛthagjana).
Therefore, he did not know for himself whether he would attain Buddhahood or not.
Next, the period from Kāśyapa Śikhin Buddha to Dīpaṃkara Buddha is explained as the second asaṃkhyeya kalpa.
At that time, the Bodhisattva used seven stalks of blue lotuses to make an offering to Dīpaṃkara Buddha;
he spread out his deerskin garment and laid his hair over the mud.
Then, Dīpaṃkara Buddha bestowed upon him this prediction:
"In a future age, you shall certainly attain Buddhahood;
your name shall be Śākyamuni."
At that time, although the Bodhisattva was able to know for himself that he would certainly become a Buddha,
he did not verbally declare, "I shall become a Buddha.
This is said to be the cultivation of the six perfections through the wisdom of the stage of Heat (uṣmagata).
Why is this? Because by means of the general perception of the four foundations of mindfulness,
one first attains the wholesome, out-flowing five aggregates.
This refers to the stage of the initial mind of the "nature-ground" (gotrabhūmi) and "conformity-patience" (anulomikī-kṣānti).
Since one already possesses faith in the realized Dharma,
one will certainly know that one shall become a Buddha.
Yet, practicing the six perfections with a warm understanding,
he did not speak of them to others because his mind was not yet clear.
Next, it clarifies [his practice] from the time of Dīpaṃkara Buddha.
Upon reaching the time of Vipaśyin Buddha,
the third asaṃkhyeya kalpa was completed;
at that time, the Bodhisattva clearly knew within his own mind that he would become a Buddha.
He spoke these words himself without any hesitation or fear:
"In a future age, I shall attain Buddhahood.
This is now called the stage of the *mūrdha* (Summit) Dharma.
By practicing the six pāramitās and contemplating the Four Noble Truths, one’s understanding becomes clear and distinct.
It is like standing on a mountain peak and looking in all four directions with clarity;
one clearly knows for oneself that one will become a Buddha.
He also spoke thus to others.
Having passed through three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas,
he planted the karma for the thirty-two marks.
Now it is said that this is the stage of entering the lower level of patience (*kṣānti*).
By employing this wisdom of patience, one practices the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) and accomplishes a hundred merits (*puṇya*).
One hundred merits are used to produce one mark;
this serves as the karmic cause for the thirty-two marks.
One plants the karmic causes for the thirty-two marks.
In the stage of the lower patience (*mṛdu-kṣānti*),
one cultivates the six *pāramitās* to accomplish the marks of a hundred merits,
which serve as the karmic causes for the thirty-two marks.
These are the thirty-two marks [of a Great Man].
Among the humans of Jambudvīpa in the desire realm,
he receives a male body.
When a Buddha appears in the world, one plants [the seeds] by means of the physical marks of the Buddha’s body.
A question is asked:
What is meant by the statement that one hundred merits produce one mark?
How many merits constitute the merit of one mark?
The answer is that different interpretations vary.
It is difficult to determine definitively.
Some say that this merit is immeasurable and beyond analogy; it is the merit of a bodhisattva who has entered the three asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
By cultivating the great practices of the mind, one plants the causes and conditions for these thirty-two marks;
for this reason, the merit is immeasurable and can be known only by a Buddha.
Question:
At what time does the Bodhisattva plant the seeds for the thirty-two marks? Answer:
At the slowest, it takes one hundred kalpas;
at the fastest, ninety-one kalpas.
Buddha Puṣya observed that Śākyamuni Bodhisattva’s own being was ripe for discipleship.
Maitreya Bodhisattva was born from among his own mature disciples.
While many people are difficult to transform, one person is easy to convert;
thus, at the Jewel Cave, Puṣya Buddha [taught him].
Light was emitted, illuminating Śākyamuni.
Following the light, the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni went to the presence of Puṣya Buddha.
For seven days and seven nights, he contemplated the Buddha with single-minded concentration.
Without blinking his eyes for even a moment,
he merely offered praise with a single verse, saying:
"Heaven and earth, this realm, and the many gateways of the chamber."
The palace of the departed is nowhere in the ten directions;
the Great Śramaṇa, the Bull-King among men,
has searched the earth, mountains, and forests, yet finds no one his equal.
By the power of his ascetic practices,
he transcended nine kalpas and attained perfect enlightenment prior to Maitreya Bodhisattva.
Regarding the fourth point, the fulfillment of the six pāramitās:
Question:
How is the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā) fulfilled? Answer:
They are able to give everything without any obstruction;
even when giving their own bodies, their minds feel no stinginess,
just like King Śibi.
He offered his own body to a pigeon, having had his skin and flesh sliced away.
Although he endured great suffering,
he placed his entire body upon the scales to redeem the life of the pigeon, his heart free from regret or resentment.
"May my body be restored to its former state if I have made this vow and can personally attest that my heart is free from regret.
Having thus made the vow, [his body was restored].
Heaven and earth shook, yet his body returned to its former state.
In such ways did these Bodhisattvas, in their past lives, sacrifice their bodies and lives as gifts,
their minds never wavering or regretting.
This is the fulfillment of the perfection of giving (dānapāramitā). Question:
How is the perfection of ethical discipline (śīlapāramitā) fulfilled?
The answer is:
One protects and upholds the pure precepts without begrudging even one's own body or life,
as did King Sudāma.
This king was diligent in maintaining his precepts and always relied upon truthful speech.
He made an appointment with the great king Kalmāṣapāda,
requesting a leave of absence to return to his own kingdom for seven days to complete his offerings to the śramaṇas.
He then came to his end;
for that king’s term had expired because he maintained the precept of truthful speech.

As can be understood from the preceding analogy, non-arising is emptiness;
