Regarding the five clarities and ten stages (*pañcavidyā-daśabhūmi*): these constitute the stage of the noble lineage (*āryagotra*). From this stage, one beholds the Buddha.
By nature,
one gives rise to the contemplation of the Middle Way and the Ultimate Truth (paramārtha-satya),
illuminating both truths simultaneously so that mind and mind cease in tranquility.
Spontaneously flowing into the ocean of *samyak-saṃbodhi*,
one realizes the unconditioned Four Noble Truths;
the single reality of the equal *dharmadhātu* is perfectly interfused.
From the first stage (bhūmi) up to the Buddha-stage,
ignorance is severed throughout;
however, based on their respective positions, they are divided into three paths.
The first stage is called the Path of Seeing the Truths (darśanamārga).
The second through the sixth stages are termed the Path of Cultivation (bhāvanāmārga).
From the seventh stage onward, [it is the Path of No-More-Learning].
This is called the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*).
As for the ten stages (*bhūmi*):
the first is the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).
2. The Ground of Freedom from Defilement;
3. The Ground of Luminous Wisdom;
4. The Ground of Blazing Wisdom.
The fifth is the Ground Difficult to Conquer;
the sixth is the Ground of Manifestation;
the seventh is the Ground of Far-Going.
The eighth is the Immovable Ground (Acalā-bhūmi).
The ninth is the Ground of Excellent Intelligence (Sādhumatī-bhūmi).
The tenth is the Ground of the Dharma Cloud (Dharmameghā-bhūmi).
These ten are collectively termed "grounds" (*bhūmi*) for two reasons:
first, they are able to generate and sustain the Buddha’s wisdom, remaining immovable;
second, they are able to bear the burden of all beings through unconditional great compassion (*nirālamba-mahākaruṇā*).
Therefore, it is called a "ground" (*bhūmi*).
As for the first ground, the Joyful (*Pramuditā*), being termed the Path of Vision (*darśana-mārga*),
it refers to the initial awakening to the principle of the Buddha-nature through the true Middle Way.
Severing ignorance and the delusions of views,
he manifests the two bodies— the True and the Responsive—
and through the conditions of his response, he immediately reaches a hundred Buddha-worlds.
Manifesting the bodies of the ten dharma realms,
they enter the ground of the wisdom of the Buddhas of the three periods of time;
this is the true and great celebration of being able to benefit both oneself and others.
Therefore, it is named the Ground of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*).
The *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* states:
"The noble practices of the bodhisattva are fulfilled."
This is abiding on the stage of fearlessness;
it is the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*).
A Bodhisattva on the first stage is free from the five fears.
There is no fear of death;
no fear of failing to make a living;
no fear of the miserable realms.
There is no fear of ill repute,
nor any fear of the majesty of the great assembly.
Although the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* does not employ these specific names, [the meanings are present].
The meaning is inferred to be the same.
If one says they do not fear greed, hatred, or delusion,
it implies that there are no three poisons within.
Externally, one is free from the eight winds;
thus, there is no fear of ill repute.
If it is said that one does not fear the hells and so forth, [it is because of this].
Thus, there is no fear of the evil realms.
If one says they do not fear śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas, then there is no fear of the great assembly.
Now that you have entered this stage of fearlessness.
Seeing the Middle Way, one is free from the two types of death;
hence it is said there is no fear of death.
The eternal life of the Dharma-body manifests that there is no fear of not surviving.
Because one has attained entry into this stage,
one is then endowed with twenty-five samādhis and destroys the twenty-five states of existence.
This reveals the nature of the self within the twenty-five states of existence.
This nature of the self is itself the true nature;
this is called the accomplishment of the practice of wisdom.
Attaining the five samādhis is the accomplishment of the five practices.
Abiding in the stage of fearlessness is what is termed the first bhūmi.
This consists of five points:
first, clarifying the accomplishment of the noble practices of the twenty-five samādhis;
second, clarifying the holy life (brahmacarya).
Third, the practice of the gods;
fourth, the practice of infants;
fifth, the practice of the sick.
First, regarding the attainment of the twenty-five samādhis and the accomplishment of noble practice,
this consists of three points.
The first is the explanation of the names of the twenty-five samādhis.
Second, the clear accomplishment of the twenty-five samādhis through correct cultivation;
third, benefiting sentient beings through external application.
First, regarding the explanation of the names of the twenty-five samādhis:
Briefly, there are four intentions;
that is, these names are established in accordance with the four *siddhāntas*.
The first is the establishment of names according to the occasion.
Second, names established according to convention;
third, names established according to their antidotes;
fourth, names established according to principle.
First, regarding names established according to circumstances:
for example, suppose a person has twenty-five sons;
they are given single-character names according to the circumstances of the time.
For the elder, one character is written at birth;
for the younger, another character is written later.
One cannot perceive the name of the elder son;
this also causes the second [son] to be called by that same name.
In this way, there is no confusion.
These twenty-five names are likewise;
each name is cited individually so that worldly convention (*saṃvṛti*) may not be confused.
All worldly designations are of this nature.
One cannot seek a fixed, ultimate reality [for these names].
Second, they are established according to the convenience of the twenty-five states of existence (*pañcaviṃśati-bhava*).
If one were to employ other names, the practical application of their meaning would not be inconvenient.
Therefore, names are established according to convenience.
Third, the twenty-five samādhis are named according to their respective antidotes;
since each counteracts a specific affliction, they are named after these antidotes.
Fourth, regarding the establishment of names according to principle:
these twenty-five samādhis do not transcend the principle of the dharma-nature;
thus, the principle accords with their meaning.
Names are established based on their meanings;
although names and meanings differ, in principle they are not distinct.
It is in accordance with these four points that this is so.
Thus, the names of twenty-five samādhis are established.
Examining the meaning of the scriptural text,
there are many instances where the two meanings are distinguished according to principle through the application of antidotes.
Thus, the names of the twenty-five samādhis are established.
Second, regarding the correct explanation of the cultivation and accomplishment of these twenty-five samādhis:
within each individual samādhi, there are four points of significance.
First, emerging from the various existences, karmic actions, afflictions, and hindrances;
second, employing samādhi to subdue and destroy them;
third, consolidating and perfecting the samādhi.
The four types of compassion destroy existence (*bhava*).
Each one fully possesses these four intentions.
First, it clarifies how the stainless samādhi (*vimala-samādhi*) destroys the existence of the hells.
This constitutes four points.
First, regarding the clarification of karmic fetters:
among all offenses, none is more grievous than those leading to hell.
There are the stains of heavy evil karma, the stains of views and afflictions (*kleśa*), the sands-like stains of [subtle] defilements, and the stains of ignorance (*avidyā*).
Second, regarding the application of samādhi to destroy ignorance:
it is for the sake of destroying these various stains that the bodhisattva practices.
By practicing the fundamental precepts mentioned previously, one purifies the defilements of evil karma;
by practicing the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*) and other concentrations mentioned previously, one suppresses the defilements of views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*);
and by practicing the wisdoms of conditioned arising and non-arising, one eradicates the defilements of views and afflictions.
Cultivating immeasurable wisdom destroys the defilements as numerous as grains of dust;
cultivating unconditioned wisdom destroys the defilement of ignorance.
As for the one who has perfected the three types of supernormal knowledge through samādhi:
Because the defilements of views and afflictions are destroyed, the samādhi of ultimate truth is accomplished;
because the defilements of evil karma and the defilements as numerous as motes of dust are destroyed,
the samādhi of conventional truth is accomplished.
Because the defilement of ignorance is destroyed,
the Samādhi of the Middle Way and the Ultimate Truth is accomplished;
through the fourfold clarity, one practices compassion to benefit all beings.
Because the Bodhisattva has already shattered the defilements of hell for himself, he attains the Samādhi of the Three Truths.
Possessing great compassion that permeates the Dharma-realm,
sentient beings possess the karmic conditions to respond to this compassion.
By the power of the King Samādhi,
although the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is immovable, it can respond to them;
as in the case of Vasu and Devadatta.
One should enter hell;
according to what is appropriate for them,
one preaches the Dharma to shatter the existence of hell.
As clarified in the "Chapter on Noble Conduct," by personally cultivating the various practices of morality, meditative concentration, and wisdom,
one personally realizes the three truths and achieves samādhi.
Within the noble practices, there is the vow of compassion; therefore,
one destroys the defilements upon the three truths of others,
as well as the defilements of evil karma and afflictions upon those same three truths.
Since one is oneself free from defilement and causes others to be free from defilement,
this samādhi is called the "Stainless Samādhi."
Therefore, the following section possesses these four points, which can be understood by analogy with what precedes.
Next, regarding the explanation of how the non-retrogressive samādhi destroys existence as an animal:
animals lack shame and dread of blame.
One falls away from the wholesome path due to the arising of unwholesome karma;
one falls away due to views and afflictions;
and one falls away due to the dust-like [afflictions].
One falls back because of ignorance.
To destroy all such fallings back, the bodhisattva cultivates ethical discipline and patience to destroy the falling back caused by evil karma.
By practicing meditative concentration, one subdues the regression caused by views and afflictions;
by cultivating the wisdom of conditioned arising and cessation, as well as the wisdom of non-arising,
one destroys the regression caused by views and afflictions.
By cultivating immeasurable wisdom, one overcomes the regression caused by [delusions as numerous as] motes of dust;
by cultivating unconditioned wisdom, one overcomes the regression caused by ignorance.
Because the delusions of views and thought are destroyed, one attains non-regression from the stage and accomplishes samādhi.
Because the dust-like sands [of afflictions] are destroyed, the Samādhi of Non-retrogression in Practice is accomplished;
because ignorance is destroyed, the Samādhi of Non-retrogression in Mindfulness is accomplished.
Thus, by the power of one's own cultivation, the three types of retrogression are overcome.
One achieves the three non-regressions and personally attains the samādhi of the three truths.
Through the power of compassion, one silently permeates the Dharma-realm.
According to the karmic conditions and capacities of sentient animals,
he may manifest as the body of an elephant king, a woodpecker, or a great vulture;
he is born among them in accordance with what is appropriate for each.
Manifesting in order to preach the Dharma and destroy the existence of animals,
one personally does not regress and causes others not to regress;
therefore, this samādhi is called the "Non-regressing Samādhi."
Next, regarding those in the existence of hungry ghosts who are liberated through the Samādhi of Joyful Mind:
the existence of hungry ghosts is constantly entangled by the evil karma of stinginess, and they suffer from the hunger of craving and the suffering of the afflictions of views and thoughts.
There is the suffering of ignorance as vast as the sands of the Ganges; there is the suffering of being obscured by the darkness of nescience.
The Bodhisattva acts to destroy all such sufferings.
Cultivating the precepts and giving destroys the suffering of stinginess and evil karma;
cultivating meditative concentration subdues the suffering of views and afflictions;
and cultivating wisdom regarding arising and ceasing destroys the suffering of views and afflictions.
Cultivating immeasurable wisdom breaks the suffering of dust-like sands;
cultivating unconditioned wisdom breaks the suffering of ignorance.
By breaking the suffering of views and thoughts, the blissful samādhi of the true dharma and the unconditioned mind is accomplished.
By destroying the dust-like suffering of stinginess and evil karma,
one accomplishes the samādhi of mental joy through various conventional classifications.
By destroying the suffering of ignorance, one accomplishes the samādhi of eternal bliss within the Middle Way.
Through his own practice, he has realized the three joys, the three truths, and samādhi;
permeated by the power of compassion within all conditioned phenomena,
he manifests in the forms and voices of various hungry ghosts.
Having caused them to be fully satisfied by means of giving, he preaches the Dharma for them,
causing them to destroy the three kinds of suffering and attain the three kinds of happiness;
thus the Bodhisattva himself attains this happiness.
Furthermore, it causes others to attain happiness;
therefore, this samādhi is called the "Samādhi of Mental Happiness.
Next is the "Samādhi of Joy."
To destroy the asuras.
There are asuras who fear many acts of anger and evil karma;
they fear views and thoughts, fear as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and fear ignorance.
In order to destroy these various fears,
the bodhisattva maintains the precepts and exerts diligence to cultivate all practices; thus,
they do not break their joy, but rather destroy the fear of evil karma.
Cultivating the joy of meditative concentration subdues the fears of views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*).
Cultivating wisdom regarding arising-and-ceasing and non-arising-and-non-ceasing attains the joy of awakening and breaks the fear of views and afflictions.
Cultivating the joy of the mirror-like reflection and immeasurable wisdom breaks the fear of the sands of *rajas*.
By cultivating non-conceptual wisdom (*anabhisaṃskāra-prajñā*), one destroys the fear of ignorance;
because the afflictions of view and thought are destroyed, the samādhi of joy in true emptiness (*śūnyatā-prāmodya-samādhi*) is accomplished;
and because the dust-like sands of evil karma are destroyed.
The Samādhi of All Sentient Beings Rejoicing is accomplished.
Because ignorance is destroyed, the Samādhi of the King of Joy is accomplished through the power of one's own practice.
Having attained such a Samādhi of Joyful Delight in the Three Truths,
through the power of compassion within all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*),
they perfume and cultivate themselves as *asuras* and are born therein.
He tames them with gentle speech and preaches the Dharma for them;
he destroys the existence of asuras and causes them to attain fearlessness.
He himself is free from the three fears and has personally realized the three joys.
It causes others to be free from fear and causes others to attain joy; therefore,
this samādhi is named the Samādhi of Joy.
The next day, the Samādhi of Light breaks through those who exist in Pūrvavideha.
Because the sun first rises in the east, it is named accordingly.
The sun is a metaphor for the light of wisdom, which is able to illuminate the darkness of delusion.
It shatters the darkness of evil karma;
it shatters the dust-like and river-sand-like darkness of views and thoughts;
and it shatters the darkness of ignorance.
In order to illuminate these various delusions and darknesses, the bodhisattva cultivates the light of the precepts of virtuous karma,
the flowing light of meditative concentration,
and the light of all-knowledge regarding both arising-and-ceasing and non-arising-non-ceasing.
The light of the knowledge of the paths arises;
the light of the knowledge of all modes arises.
As clarity is born, darkness is extinguished.
One destroys the darkness of evil karma with the light of virtuous precepts;
one destroys the darkness of views and afflictions with the light of meditative concentration;
and one destroys the darkness of views and afflictions with the light of both arising-and-ceasing and non-arising-non-ceasing.
One cultivates the light of the immeasurable knowledge of the aspects of the path to shatter the darkness as numerous as motes of dust;
one cultivates the light of unconditioned omniscience to shatter the darkness of ignorance.
Because it destroys the darkness of views and afflictions,
the Samādhi of the Sunlight of All-Knowledge is accomplished;
because it destroys the darkness of the sands of dust, [the Samādhi of the Moonlight of Non-Obstruction is accomplished].
The Samādhi of the Sunlight of the Knowledge of the Paths is accomplished because it destroys the darkness of ignorance.
The Samādhi of the Sunlight of the Knowledge of All Modes is accomplished.
By the power of his practice, he personally realized these three truths and samādhis;
by the power of his compassion, he permeated the continent of Pūrvavideha,
manifesting there to preach the Dharma and shatter its threefold delusions.
Because it manifests the sun of the wisdom of the three truths,
this samādhi is named the Sunlight Samādhi.
Next, as for the Moonlight Samādhi, which destroys those who exist in Aparagoyānī:
When the moon first arises, its light appears in the west;
this is a name established according to its location.
Furthermore, the moonlight is also a metaphor for dispelling darkness.
The three samādhis and four intentions are explained.
The *sūryaprabha-samādhi* (sunlight samādhi) may be understood by analogy.
Next, the *jvālana-samādhi* (flame samādhi) destroys those who exist in Uttarakuru.
The north is a region of darkness where ice freezes and is difficult to melt;
it will not melt unless by hot flames.
Such is the case for the people of Uttarakuru.
Those who cling to ice-like notions of self and what belongs to self are difficult to transform and deliver;
they cannot be heated by the blazing flames of the fire of wisdom.
The mind that clings to "self" and "what belongs to self" can never be eliminated;

rather, it is the refutation of "self" and "what belongs to self" that constitutes the principle of the non-existence of self and what belongs to self. This [refutation] is merely a conceptual construction of non-self and non-belonging.
In reality, there still exists a nature:
the delusion of a personal self,
the delusion of a phenomenal self, and the delusion of a true-self.
The ice of hibernation has not yet melted.
To shatter these various delusions of a self and their frozen attachments,
the Bodhisattva cultivates the wisdom of true non-self, such as that which pertains to arising and ceasing.
One cultivates the wisdom of the four truths with measure to destroy the delusion regarding the self-nature of persons;
one cultivates the wisdom of the four truths without effort to destroy the delusion regarding the self-nature of phenomena.
The delusion regarding the self of true suchness is destroyed.
If one attains the flame of wisdom that realizes the emptiness of the person,
the delusion regarding the self of substantiality is destroyed.
The samādhi of true reality is accomplished;
one attains the flaming wisdom of the emptiness of true dharmas and destroys the delusions regarding the self of phenomena.
Having attained the Samādhi of the Conventional Truth (saṃvṛti-satya),
one is thus able to be like a tree growing from a seed within space;
this is because emptiness accords with the conventional in order to transform sentient beings.
One attains the flame of the wisdom of true suchness and selflessness,
which destroys the delusions regarding a self within true suchness,
knowing that there is neither "self" nor "non-self."
This is the meaning of the true self.
Within the dharma of non-self, there is a true self;
this is precisely seeing the nature of the self in Uttarakuru.
Thereupon, the samādhi is accomplished;
mind after mind is quiescent.
The Bodhisattva personally realizes the samādhi of the three truths.
By the power of compassion, he manifests the form and voice of Uttarakuru,
destroying the northern notion of "no-self" and "mine," and causing beings to realize the samādhi of the true self.
Therefore, this samādhi is named the "Blazing Fire Samādhi.
Next, regarding the "Illusion-like Samādhi" which destroys those who exist in Jambudvīpa:
in the south, the retributions are manifold and diverse.
Life is short and uncertain,
like a magical illusion;
this is the fruit of evil karma produced by the illusions of the mind.
Delusions produce afflictions; delusions produce ignorance;
delusions produce nescience.
All sentient beings do not know that these are like illusions.
Now, in order to destroy these various illusions, the Bodhisattva cultivates three kinds of samādhi.
By cultivating the Samādhi of True Reality, he produces the outflow-free (anāsrava) state as an illusion,
thereby destroying the illusions of views and afflictions (dṛṣṭi-kleśa).
By practicing the samādhi of conventional truth, one produces the knowledge of the modes of the path as an illusion and destroys the illusion of ignorance;
by practicing the samādhi of the Middle Way, one produces the knowledge of all modes as an illusion.
One shatters the illusion of ignorance.
Through the power of cultivation, one personally realizes the samādhi of the three truths;
through the power of compassion, one shatters the power of others.
Therefore, it is called the Illusion-like Samādhi (*māyopama-samādhi*).
Next is the Immovable Samādhi (*acala-samādhi*),
which destroys those who exist as the Four Heavenly Kings.
This deva protects the land;
as he wanders through the world, his physical retribution is in flux.
This, then, is the movement of karmic fruition.
The movement of views and thoughts is the movement of ignorance;
the movement of a single mind cultivating goodness is non-movement,
as is the cultivation of the liberations (*vimokṣa*) and other non-moving karmas.
The immovability of the wisdom that destroys retribution counters the movement of karma; the immovability of true wisdom counters the movement of views and afflictions;
the immovability of the wisdom that issues forth into the provisional counters the movement of ignorance.
The wisdom of the Middle Way is as immovable as the summit of Mount Sumeru;
by the power of cultivation, it shatters the movement of ignorance and personally realizes the three kinds of immovability.
By the power of compassion,
one destroys the three types of movement of others;
therefore, this samādhi is called the Immovable Samādhi.
Next, regarding the Samādhi of the Difficult-to-Subdue which destroys the existence of the Heaven of the Thirty-three:
this heaven is situated at the summit of the four heavens;
it is thus a retribution that is difficult to subdue.
Views and afflictions are difficult to subdue; ignorance is difficult to subdue;
and nescience is difficult to subdue.
The Bodhisattva acts to shatter their haughty pride.
Therefore, one cultivates ethical discipline, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
One destroys the retribution that is difficult to subdue;
one cultivates both the arising-and-ceasing and the non-arising-and-non-ceasing.
Therefore, by the power of one's own practice, the three types of difficult-to-subdue [afflictions] are subdued; and by the power of compassion,
the three types of difficult-to-subdue [afflictions] belonging to others are destroyed.
Therefore, this samādhi is named "Difficult to Subdue.
Next, regarding the samādhi "Delighting the Mind," it destroys the existence of the Yāma devas;
these devas have no fear of swords or clubs in the void.
To take this as joy is truly not joy;
there is no joy that does not involve the karma of movement.
There has been no joy of the untainted (anāsrava),
no joy of the knowledge of the modes of the path (mārgākārajñatā),
and no joy of the middle way.
In order to destroy this,
the bodhisattva cultivates the contemplation of the Four Noble Truths and the meditative joy within the eight liberations (*aṣṭau vimokṣāḥ*) to overcome that agitation,
distraction, and lack of joy.
The wisdom of arising and ceasing destroys the dissatisfaction of those with outflows;
the immeasurable wisdom destroys the dissatisfaction of those who sink into emptiness;
the wisdom of non-action destroys the dissatisfaction of those who cling to the two extremes.
Because of the joy of non-arising, the samādhi of ultimate truth is accomplished;
because of the joy of emerging into the conventional to accord with capacities, the samādhi of conventional truth is accomplished;
and because of the joy of the Middle Way, the samādhi of the Middle Way is accomplished.
Through the power of one's own practice, one personally realizes and accomplishes samādhi;
through the power of compassion, one shatters the samādhis of others and brings them to accomplishment.
Therefore, it is called the "Pleasing Samādhi" (Ramaṇīya-samādhi).
Next, regarding the blue-colored samādhi that destroys existence in the Tuṣita Heaven:
the karmic retribution and pleasures of this heaven are blue, and its eyes and ornaments are all blue.
The Bodhisattva, in order to destroy this existence, [practices this samādhi].
Therefore, one cultivates the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
It is not that the non-blue is truly seen as blue;
it is not that the non-blue is conventionally seen as blue.
Therefore, one attains the Middle Way.
By perceiving the Middle Way within the blue, one shatters the existence of that blue;
this principle may be inferred accordingly.
Next, the yellow samādhi destroys existence in the Nirmāṇarati Heaven;
next, the red samādhi destroys existence in the Paranirmitavaśavartin Heaven.
These may be understood by analogy with the preceding blue samādhi.
Next, regarding the white samādhi that destroys the existence of the first dhyāna:
the first dhyāna is free from the five hindrances and unwholesome states of the desire realm;
it is thus a wholesome and pure state of concentrated mind.
However, as long as one has not yet abandoned the darkness of the views and afflictions (*kleśa*), the dust-like [afflictions],
and ignorance (*avidyā*), the Bodhisattva, in order to destroy these various dark practices,
cultivates the white dharmas of the three truths.
The meaning of breaking the precepts can be understood by inference.
Next, regarding the various samādhis that destroy the existence of the Brahmā King:
the Brahmā King presides over a trichiliocosm.
Since the categories within the trichiliocosm are manifold,
there are various designations;
in order to dismantle these manifoldnesses, one cultivates various forms of emptiness.
Entering into various conventional designations,
one perceives the various middle ways;
the Tathāgatagarbha contains manifold things within it.
This is called the Samādhi of Various Aspects;
its meaning can be inferred through reasoning.
Next, regarding the Samādhi of Simultaneous Illumination which destroys the existence of the Second Dhyāna:
Because the second dhyāna alone possesses the two factors of internal clarity (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*) and joy (*prīti*),
it receives these two names together.
It is in order to break through this duality that the Bodhisattva [proceeds].
Cultivating the dual emptiness, the dual provisional, and the dual middle,
and illuminating the two sovereigns simultaneously—
the meaning may be inferred from this.
Next, as for those who break through the existence of the third dhyāna by means of the Thunder-Sound Samādhi:
this dhyāna receives pleasure that is foremost among all;
becoming deeply attached to this pleasure, they remain like fish in ice or hibernating insects.
In order to shatter this pleasure,
the Bodhisattva uses the thunderous sound of the Three Truths to startle and terrify them;
this can be understood through careful analysis.
Next, regarding the "Rain Shower Samādhi" which destroys those who possess the four dhyānas:
the four dhyānas are like the great earth, which possesses various kinds of sprouts;
if they do not receive rain, the sprouts will not grow.
All roots of goodness exist within the four dhyānas;
if the three truths and the three knowledges rain down, they will be well-generated.
The meaning can be understood through inference.
Next, regarding the breaking of existence in the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñisattva*) by means of the Space-like Samādhi (*ākāśasamādhi*):
this refers to the fact that the heavens of the non-Buddhists are not actually the Heaven of No-Thought.
Yet they calculate this to be the nirvana of non-conception,
like a child dreaming of urination;
it is for the sake of destroying this [view] that the Bodhisattva acts.

Because the emptiness of the three truths destroys the state of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñika*), it is said to be like the samādhi of empty space. Next, the mirror-like samādhi destroys the existence of *nānāvyañjana* (the realm of subtle form).
By practicing the perfumed dhyāna, one is born according to that dhyāna.
Although one may attain pure form, one cannot know it;
form is like a reflection in a mirror.
The bodhisattva knows that form is like a reflection in a mirror, and thus is empty.
By discerning the infinite images based upon the mirror,
one immediately perceives the Middle Way within the fundamental nature;
thus, one accomplishes the Samādhi of the Three Truths and shatters the containment of the *nāma-rūpa*.
Next, regarding the unimpeded samādhi that destroys existence within the sphere of infinite space:
in this state, one attains the ability to emerge from the cage of form and float about without obstruction.
However, this is not yet the unimpededness of the samādhi of the three truths.
There are obstacles of views and thoughts, obstacles of the dust-like afflictions, and obstacles of ignorance.
The Bodhisattva cultivates the samādhi of the three truths to break these various obstacles;
therefore, it is called the "Unobstructed Samādhi. Next, the "Samādhi of Constant Illumination" breaks the station of consciousness.
If there were a continuity of consciousness that was uninterrupted, it would be impermanent.
To destroy this notion of impermanence,
the bodhisattva cultivates the contemplation of the permanence based on enumeration.
The continuity of transformative function is constantly subverted by the eternally serene Buddha-nature.
Next, regarding the subversion of those who dwell in the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*) through the samādhi of joy:
this sphere of nothingness is like delusion.
Because of delusion, this is suffering.
By means of the samādhi of the three truths and three contemplations,
the Bodhisattva breaks through [delusion] and attains the bliss of the samādhi of the three truths.
This is the Samādhi of Delight, which follows my Samādhi and destroys the existence of the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception.
The beings in this heaven consider its summit to be Nirvāṇa and the true self;
the Bodhisattva perceives this.
There still remain subtle afflictions and a lack of mastery;
that is to say, there is a lack of mastery over the afflictions of views and thought,
as well as a lack of mastery over the *rajas* (dust-like) afflictions.
Ignorance is not autonomous;
how could it be the self?
It is for the purpose of refuting this self [that this is taught].
Cultivate the Samādhi of the Three Truths to break through this [clinging],
so that one may attain non-self. Yet,
in accordance with worldly convention, there is the "self" and the eightfold self-mastering self.
For this reason, it is called the Samādhi of Me.
The Samādhi of the Twenty-five Existences uses itself to eliminate the twenty-five samādhis.
Within a single existence, all three truths are fully present.
The Samādhi Bodhisattva personally cultivates the samādhi of the three truths,
thereby personally eliminating the delusions regarding the three truths within the twenty-five realms of existence;
by the power of compassion, he...
By eliminating the delusions regarding the twenty-five existences and the three truths of others,
one thereby attains the names of the twenty-five samādhis; or,
it may arise from the foundation of non-abiding.
Based on the four *siddhāntas*, twenty-five names are established.
As it is said:
"In general, the term 'samādhi' is named 'tuning and straightening the mind' (*tiao-zhi-ding*)."
The samādhi of ultimate truth is made straight by being free from craving and views;
the samādhi of conventional truth is made straight by conforming to the capacities [of beings];
the samādhi of the Middle Way is made straight by being devoid of the crookedness of the two extremes.
Therefore, all are called samādhis.
If one merely enters emptiness directly, it is not the direct [path].
When a śrāvaka attains entry into emptiness, it is not the sovereign samādhi (rājasamādhi).
If one enters the provisional, it is likewise not ultimate.
Although a bodhisattva attains the knowledge of the modes of the path,
they are still not said to have attained the King Samādhi.
Because he has attained the samādhi of the Middle Way, he is called the King;
for within each of the twenty-five samādhis,
there is the samādhi of the Middle Way.
Therefore, they are called the twenty-five samādhis,
all of which are king-samādhis.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
These twenty-five samādhis are called the Kings of All Samādhis.
If one enters the King Samādhi, all samādhis enter therein.
Therefore, when a bodhisattva dwells in the Immovable Ground (Acalā-bhūmi),
they fully attain these various powers and functions of the twenty-five samādhis; for instance,
they can place the high and vast Mount Sumeru within a mustard seed.
They manifest and vanish with sovereign mastery through transformation;
they can enter the hells without undergoing sufferings such as the disintegration of the body.
If one’s noble practice is perfected, such things are possible.
This is exactly as explained in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
Regarding the external application of the three types of supernormal knowledge (*trividyā*) for the benefit of others,
this refers to the two kinds of benefit consisting of the ability to manifest and conceal oneself.
He enters the King of Samādhis,
wherein all kings of samādhis are fully contained.
For this reason, all sentient beings undergo various sufferings and afflictions.
With single-minded devotion, they take refuge and invoke the name, seeking protection.
The Bodhisattva, abiding in samādhi, immediately contemplates that the three karmas are all brought to liberation.
There are eight kinds of liberation.
First, it destroys the suffering of the retributive fruits within the twenty-five states of existence;
second, it destroys the suffering of the causes within the twenty-five states of existence;
third, it destroys the suffering of the afflictions of view and thought (dṛṣṭi-kleśa and bhāvanā-kleśa) within the twenty-five states of existence as experienced by the śrāvakas.
Fourth, it shatters the suffering of the view-and-thought afflictions within the twenty-five states of existence for Pratyekabuddhas.
Fifth, it shatters the suffering of the view-and-thought afflictions within the twenty-five states of existence for Śrāvaka Bodhisattvas.

Sixth, it shatters the suffering of the afflictions of view and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāva-kleśa*) within the twenty-five states of existence for those of the three vehicles who follow the Shared Teaching.
Seventh, it shatters the suffering of the countless delusions of ignorance regarding the twenty-five states of existence for Bodhisattvas of the Distinct Teaching.
The eight obstacles [of the *pāramitā* teachings] break through the delusions of ignorance and suffering within the twenty-five existences and the three truths of the Perfect Teaching Bodhisattva;
that by single-mindedly invoking the Name one attains liberation is precisely what is intended here.
Therefore, it is said that the twenty-five samādhis can destroy the twenty-five states of existence (*bhava*).
Second, the manifestation of benefits:
This refers to abiding in the twenty-five samādhis.
When the karmic conditions of sentient beings within the ten dharma realms arise to evoke a response,
the Universal Manifestation Body (Sambhogakāya) appears eightfold to bestow happiness upon those beings.
It is like the manifestation of supernatural powers through the Universal Gate of Avalokiteśvara.
If there are sentient beings who should be liberated by means of a Buddha’s body, [the Bodhisattva appears] in that form.
This refers to being able to manifest the body and preach the Dharma through the eight phases of attaining enlightenment;
it is precisely this sutra’s clarification of dwelling in inconceivable liberation and manifesting various transformations.
This Bodhisattva fulfills the noble practices of the first stage and possesses great loving-kindness and great compassion that are without objective conditions,
just as a magnet attracts iron.
Second, regarding the pure conduct (*brahmacarya*):
this refers to the four immeasurables—compassion, loving-kindness, sympathetic joy, and equanimity—without an objective referent.
The Bodhisattva, by means of the mind of Great Nirvana, [cultivates these].
By practicing the noble conduct, one attains the stage of fearlessness.
Therein lie twenty-five samādhis of boundless and great function.
At that time, compassion is the true brahmacarya.
This is not the cultivation of the four immeasurable minds practiced by other Brahmās,
nor is it the compassion directed toward sentient beings or phenomena as taught in the Tripiṭaka or the Shared Teachings.
At that time, the Bodhisattva,
through this compassion that is objectless and thought-free,
cultivates the practices for sentient beings until they are all accomplished and perfected.
This Brahma-conduct is itself all dharmas.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"Loving-kindness is the Tathāgata; compassion is Buddha-nature."
If compassion were not fully perfected,
the ten powers, the thirty-two marks, and the four fearlessnesses would not belong to the Tathāgata; therefore,
they are not the compassion of the Tathāgata.
The power of wisdom is vast and profound, capable of fulfilling all merits and virtues;
this self-adornment is called the Brahma-conduct (*brahmacarya*).
As for the three types of supernormal knowledge (*vidyā*) and the conduct of the heavens:
This is precisely the Middle Way, the ultimate celestial realm—
the natural principle wherein practice manifests the principle, and the principle brings practice to fulfillment.
Therefore, principle is called "the movement of heaven.
Although a bodhisattva enters the first stage,
they should not dwell in that first stage.
Because there is something to be attained,
one should further cultivate the wisdom of the higher stages.
Tenfold, one gives rise to true cultivated wisdom (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*), accords with principle, manifests principle, and accomplishes practice.
It is called "divine conduct" (*devacara*).
Divine conduct is the adornment of wisdom;
pure conduct (*brahmacarya*) is the adornment of merit.
Seeking the Buddha-way above,
there are thus the Holy Practice and the Celestial Practice;
transforming sentient beings below, there are the Brahma Practice, the Illness Practice, and the Infant Practice.
Fourth, regarding the practice of the infant:
if a bodhisattva’s merit and wisdom increase further,
then the true mark becomes even more manifest.
Although one does not intentionally direct the mind toward benefiting sentient beings,
one spontaneously possesses both hidden and manifest benefits;
through the power of celestial conduct, there is hidden benefit.
Through the power of the holy life (brahmacarya), there is manifest benefit;
sentient beings may possess the potential for minor roots of goodness,
yet these cannot grow unless developed by a bodhisattva.
By the power of the roots of goodness of kindness and compassion,
like a magnet attracting iron,
they harmonize their light and skillful conduct so that sentient beings may perceive them.
The Bodhisattva begins together with those who are first learning;
he gradually cultivates the five precepts and the ten wholesome actions that lead to the retributive fruits of the human and celestial realms,
including the practice of the "willow-leaf" observance of the Heaven of the Thirty-three.
Furthermore, he demonstrated the observation and cultivation of the two hundred and fifty precepts,
the four truths, the twelve links of dependent origination,
and the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment.
He acts in common with the infant-like practices of the two vehicles,
and further manifests the shared cultivation of the six perfections;
for a hundred kalpas, he plants the seeds of the marks and signs to gently subdue the afflictions.
The practice of minor virtues of the Bodhisattva of the Six Perfections,
as well as the demonstration that form is identical to emptiness— being without arising and without cessation—
is the practice of minor virtues of the Shared Teaching.
Furthermore, it demonstrates that within the provisional and distinct teachings, the gradual stages and the semblance of the Middle Way—
even minor acts of goodness—
are all the power of a compassionate mind.
Bending down to accord with the multitude of beings, he uplifts and brings them to accomplishment;
from his heart he bestows joy and initiates the conduct of an infant,
as stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
An infant is able to utter great words,
namely "Bha" and "Ho."
This is identical to the six perfections (ṣaṭpāramitā).
Although the six perfections are minor practices, they are called "great" because one seeks to become a Buddha;
this is what is meant by "Bhava."
Furthermore, it is said:
"Not perceiving such characteristics as day and night, or intimacy and distance, is identical to the Bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching;
this is the meaning of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) that form itself is emptiness."
It is further said:
"One is unable to perform great or small deeds;
'great deeds' refer to the five heinous crimes (*pañcānantarya*), while 'small deeds' refer to the mind of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*)."
This is identical to the Separate Teaching (biejiao), for the Separate Teaching is not [concerned with] birth-and-death;
thus, there are no five heinous crimes, and because it is not nirvana, there is no Hinayana mind.
It is further said: "The yellow leaves of the poplar tree."
This is precisely the infant of the five precepts and ten wholesome actions of humans and devas.
It is also said:
"To take what is not the Way as the Way."
Because it can produce the subtle causes and conditions for the Path,
that which is not the Path is called the Path;
this is identical to the infantile stage of the Two Vehicles.
Thus we know that the power of the great root of goodness of compassion can manifest in provisional forms to transform sentient beings,
employing minor skillful means in accordance with them.
They lead them to incline toward the Buddha-wisdom;
therefore, it is called the practice of the infant.
Fifth is the practice of the sick person.
This practice arises from unconditional great compassion.
If even a minor good deed is performed, there will inevitably be an aspect of illness.
Now, we shall distinguish this in terms of the side of goodness that arises simultaneously.
It is called the practice of an infant.
Being on the same side as the afflictions is called the practice of illness.
From the practice of illness arises the sickness of sentient beings through great compassion.
Therefore, my illness is one that permeates my heart with great compassion as I sport within the hells;
it is an illness identical to the evil karma of sentient beings,
just as when Devadatta was in hell.
Just as it is with the bliss of the third dhyāna,
so it is for animals, hungry ghosts, and asuras. Furthermore,
like humans and devas, they possess the afflictions of karmic fetters and birth, old age, sickness, and death.
Furthermore, they share with the two vehicles the affliction of the views and thoughts [of outflows].
Through skillful means, they are approached and instructed to apply themselves diligently.
This is also the case for the Bodhisattvas of the Tripiṭaka Teaching and the Shared Teaching.
Furthermore, since the illnesses of the dust-like and river-sand-like ignorance are identical to those of the Separate Teaching,
the Bodhisattva likewise accords with those illnesses to benefit sentient beings throughout the entire Dharma-realm.
This constitutes the mutual relationship of the five practices (*pañca-caryā*).

The practice of illness is precisely what is elucidated in the six chapters on the interior [of the house] within the "Inquiry into Illness" chapter (*Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra*) of this *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*.
The Bodhisattva of the first stage is fully endowed with the five practices;
these may be considered the first of the virtues.
As for the remaining nine kinds of virtue:
Alternatively, it may correspond to the nine stages.
Regarding the statement that it "destroys the delusions of ignorance and views," the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
Prior to this,
all were termed people of false views;
these were the followers of the two teachings and the three vehicles.
Since none of them have yet perceived this principle,
they are called people of false views. For this reason,
the Great Being rebuked Subhūti.
"The six masters are your teachers.
This means that the celestial Māras and non-Buddhists act as companions in labor with a single hand;
this refers even to the ten stages of faith in the Separate Teaching.
Although these [afflictions] are suppressed during the thirty stages of mind (*triṃśac-citta*),
since they have not yet been severed,
one still remains possessed of ignorance (*avidyā*) and distinct views (*pṛthag-dṛṣṭi*).
This may be the intended meaning behind the criticism of the bodhisattvas.
These two stages, from the second to the sixth bhūmi, are called the path of cultivation (bhāvanāmārga),
wherein one abandons the specific delusions and the craving of the three realms.
As clarified in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*,
when Kāśyapa heard the sound of the *kinnara* lute, he could not remain at ease and said,
"I have already severed the five desires of the three realms."
These are the five desires produced by the pure and sublime merits of a bodhisattva;
therefore, one cannot remain equanimous toward these matters.
By this analogy, craving for the form and formless realms is likewise the same.
In this sutra, the Great Being rebukes Subhūti, saying:
"You are identical to those afflicted by defilements; you have not reached the other shore."
The meaning is this: having entered the eight difficulties, one does not attain freedom from difficulty;
therefore, [this applies] from the second stage through the sixth stage.
The general name "Path of Cultivation" refers to the abandonment of these specific delusions.
Now, inferring by way of their meaning,
[this corresponds to] the second stage, the Ground Free from Defilement (vimalā-bhūmi).
The provisional severance of the desire-realm afflictions according to the Separate Teaching (Pratyekabuddha/Śrāvaka) is called the stage of the Sakṛdāgāmin-pratipannaka;
the Threefold Knowledge (Traividya) ground is the fruit of the Sakṛdāgāmin according to the Separate Teaching.
The fourth is the Stage of Blazing Flames (*Arciṣmatī-bhūmi*),
which corresponds to the stage of the *Anāgāmin*-candidate (*pratipannaka*) according to the Separate Teaching (*pratyeka-śāsana*).
The fifth is the Stage Difficult to Conquer (*Sudurjayā-bhūmi*).
This refers to the fruit of *anāgāmin* according to the Separate Teaching (*pratyeka-śāsana*),
wherein the afflictions of the distinct categories are severed and desire for the realm of sensuality is exhausted.
This corresponds to the sixth stage, the Ground of Presence (*abhimukhī-bhūmi*).
This refers to the stage of the Arhat-path candidate (arhattva-pratipannaka) in the Distinct Teaching (bhedavyavahāra),
who has severed attachment to distinct form.
Seventh is the Far-Reaching Ground (dūraṅgamā-bhūmi).
This refers to the fruit of Arhatship according to the Distinct Teaching (biejiao).
Because one has severed the distinct craving for the formless realm (*ārūpya*),
it is from this point onward designated as the Path of No-More-Learning (*aśaikṣamārga*).
Question: Against which of the four fruits (*phala*) is this contrasted? In what sutras or treatises does it appear?
Answer: Regarding the distinct teaching (*pṛthag-vyavasthāna*), the clarification of abandonment (*prahāṇa*) and suppression (*vibhava*) is contrasted with the four fruits;
the sutras and treatises on this matter are for the most part not in agreement.
The methods employed by the various Mahāyāna Dharma Masters also differ from those of the masters of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
Regarding the classification of stages according to the Shared Teaching (*pāṭha-sāmānya*), it is said:
On the first stage, one abandons views;
on the second stage, one abandons sensual desire;
on the third stage, one abandons desire for the realm of form.
In the fourth stage, one abandons craving for the formless realm.
According to the masters of the *Dilun* school, who broadly follow the fundamental tenets to determine the stages of realization,
there is a tradition that uses the abandonment of views in the [first] three stages to designate one as a *srotāpanna*.
From the fourth stage to the sixth stage is called the Sakṛdāgāmin;
the second is the master who relies on the Dharma;
the seventh stage is called the Anāgāmin.
The third reliance on the teacher is the one named Arhat,
who has attained the equal enlightenment of the ten stages.
This is the fourth reliance on the teacher.
The third stage involves the abandonment of views;
the fourth stage is called *sakṛdāgāmin*;
the fifth stage is called *anāgāmin*.
The sixth stage is called Arhat;
according to the *Renwang jing*,
the fourth stage severs [the delusions of] views, and the fifth stage is called Sakṛdāgāmin.
The sixth stage is called Anāgāmin;
the seventh stage is called Arhat.
Such various explanations differ from one another.
It is difficult to establish a definitive basis.
For now, I have inferred this meaning to provide a correspondence with the four fruits;
at first glance, it seems to accord with the convenience of the explanation.
Since there is no definitive textual authority, the Buddha’s intention is difficult to discern;
one need not dogmatically cling to a single view.
Question: For what reason are the explanations inconsistent?
Answer:
As has already been explained previously,
the eighth stage of immovability (*acalā-bhūmi*) is precisely the stage of the *pratyekabuddha* according to the Separate Teaching (*prātibhedika-śāsana*).
The Dilun masters say that this clarifies the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*),
though it is not known from which sūtras or śāstras this is derived.
Not only does one attain the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) in the eighth stage, whereby one remains in stillness yet constantly acts;
acting without marks and without effortful application of mind,
one spontaneously severs the ignorance and delusions of the dharma-realm, exhausting even the habitual tendencies of form.
Ninth is the Ground of Excellent Intelligence (*Sādhumatī-bhūmi*).
Ignorance becomes somewhat attenuated and the habitual tendencies of the mind are exhausted;
wisdom becomes increasingly clear as one skillfully enters into the true nature of reality (*tathatā*).
The tenth stage, the Cloud of Dharma (dharmameghā bhūmi),
possesses compassion and wisdom like a great cloud;
its compassion universally moistens all beings.
All are rain-clouds of wisdom;
they are able to uphold the rain of Dharma preached by all Buddhas of the ten directions and sever ignorance.
The sixth stage, the Ground of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi-bhūmi*),
is the fulfillment of ultimate wisdom (*prāntajñāna*) and entry into the gate of profound mystery (*chong-hyeon mun*).
If one looks toward it from the perspective of the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā*), it is called Buddhahood.
Aspiring toward wondrous enlightenment, they are called Bodhisattvas of the Vajra Mind, and are also called Bodhisattvas of the Stainless Ground (*vimalā-bhūmi*).
The three māras have already been exhausted; only the single category of the Lord of Death (*mṛtyu-māra*) remains.
This refers to the severing of the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of ignorance.
Question: Why did the preceding Shared Teaching (*p’ung-chiao*) not distinguish the Buddha of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambuddha*)?
Answer: Because the habitual tendencies within the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*) are easily exhausted.
Therefore, it is unnecessary to posit that the Cloud of Dharma (dharmamegha) stage emerges from Equal Enlightenment (samyaksambodhi).
Question: In the sutras and śāstras of the Separate Teaching (prthaktva-naya), why is it explained in various places that [the stages] follow after the Cloud of Dharma?
Furthermore, there is the Vajra-like Perfect Enlightenment;
its own sūtras and śāstras clarify that once the practices of the ten stages (daśabhūmi) are fulfilled,
one immediately attains the fruit of Buddhahood.
The Dharma Masters of the North and South have suppressed this argument.
In response, it is said: establishing the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*) further does not constitute an obstacle. Why is this so?
The Avataṃsaka Sūtra elucidates the merit, wisdom, and virtues of the tenth stage, the Cloud of Dharma;
using this as a comparison for the Buddha.
It is like the amount of soil on a fingernail compared to the great earth.
If that were so, although one speaks of a single category of ignorance (*avidyā*), in reality it cannot be said to be a category.
How, then, could a Bodhisattva in their final moment of mind attain the path of effortlessness (*anābhoga-mārga*)?
Its swiftness is like that of the wind;
within a single day,
it can shatter immeasurable categories of the veils and delusions of ignorance.
How much more so does the *Yingluo jing* clarify the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi-bhūmi*),
wherein for hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas one enters the gate of profound mystery and practices the affairs of ordinary beings in reverse.

Therefore, it is established that upon opening the stage of the Cloud of Dharma (dharmameghā-bhūmi), one further establishes the Vajra-mind of Equal Enlightenment; this is not erroneous from the perspective of principle.
This is because if one knows that within a single grade there are immeasurable grades of ignorance.

Since the unimpeded wisdom of the *dharmameghā-bhūmi* (Cloud of Dharma Stage) is already perfected, why would it be necessary to further establish a separate stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*)?
As for the seventh, the stage of Wondrous Enlightenment (*miao-jue-di*): [it refers to...]
At the final mind of vajra, one awakens to the vast, luminous Great Enlightenment;
when wondrous wisdom exhausts the source and the habitual tendencies of ignorance are eradicated,
this is called true liberation.
Solemn and free from all entanglements, quiescent yet ever-illuminating,
it is called the Ground of Wondrous Enlightenment (*abhisaṃbodhi-bhūmi*).
It eternally abides as the fruit of Buddhahood, fully endowed with all Buddha-dharmas.
It is called the fruit of bodhi.
Nirvāṇa, characterized by the four virtues, is called the fruit of the fruit. Question:
Is it by means of the diamond-like wisdom (*vajra-jñāna*) that one cuts off ignorance,
or is it by means of the wisdom of sublime awakening (*prajñā-jñāna*)?
The answer is:
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"One who has something to be severed is called a superior person (*sottara-pudgala*);
one who has nothing to be severed is called the unsurpassed person (*anuttara-pudgala*)."
Question: The Śrīmālā-sūtra states that the power of the ground of abiding ignorance (*avidyā-āśraya-bhūmi*) is the greatest.
It is that which can be severed by the wisdom of the Buddha’s bodhi.
The answer is:
if one employs the distinct teaching (biete jiao) that penetrates through the ten stages and the stage of Equal Enlightenment (jue).
This is precisely the wisdom of the Buddha’s bodhi. Why is this so?
As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
A Bodhisattva in the ninth stage is said to "see by hearing," while a Bodhisattva in the tenth stage is said to "see with the eye.
Although they see the Buddha-nature, it is not yet clear or distinct.
Because the path of non-obstruction coexists with the afflictions,
it is not clearly perceived.
That which the Buddhas and Tathāgatas perceive with perfect clarity is true liberation.
Because it is solemn and transcends all external conditions, it is perfectly clear.
If one explains the meaning according to the Separate Teaching (biejiao),
it begins from the first stage, the Stage of Joy (pramuditā-bhūmi).
One employs the wisdom of the Buddha’s bodhi to sever the first grade of ignorance,
continuing until it is finally and completely severed at the final moment of mind of the stage of Equal Enlightenment (samyaksambodhi).
If one clarifies the meaning according to the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao),
this refers to the first stage, the Dwelling of Initial Resolve (Chufanzhu),
wherein one attains the application of the Buddha’s Bodhi-wisdom.
One severs the ignorance of the first stage, continuing until it is completely severed at the final moment of mind prior to equal enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).

Fourth, regarding the explanation of the stages of the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* according to the Separate Teaching (*pṛthag-deśanā*): [the text here explains] the stage of the Pure and Stainless One (*vimala*).
Vimalakīrti is a Great Being (mahāsattva) who is in his final birth before Buddhahood;
he occupies the rank of a stainless Bodhisattva at the stage of the Vajra-mind of Equal Enlightenment.
Because the principle of Buddha-nature is fully manifest, he is called "Pure."
The secondary afflictions and both the active and habitual tendencies are completely exhausted;
as for the residual habit of ignorance,
it is like a wisp of smoke— though present, it is as if non-existent.
Therefore, it is called "Stainless.
With the wisdom of the ultimate limit fulfilled, it accords with profound principle within while its external application is boundless.
Within the equality of the *dharmadhātu*, it responds to conditions to carry out transformative teachings.
Therefore, it is named "Appellation" (Ghoṣa).
Thus, it is said to be the Pure and Stainless Appellation (Vimalakīrti).
How could this possibly be the same as those of the Tripiṭaka or the Shared Teachings?
This clarifies the meaning of Vimalakīrti’s purity and stainlessness.

The reason his pedagogical traces manifest as being identical to the stage of a *crown prince* (the position immediately preceding Buddhahood) is to censure the three vehicles of the Shared Teaching (*pāryāyika-yāna*).
This is the meaning of the "reception" (jue) in the Separate Teaching (biejiao) of the Mahāyāna.
*Sijiaoyi*, Scroll 14; *Jiaoyi*, Scroll 11.
Compiled by Master Zhiyi of Xiuchan Monastery on Mount Tiantai. Part Four:
Clarifying the Stages according to the Perfect Teaching. Regarding the explanation of the meaning of "Pure and Stainless":
the Perfect Teaching elucidates that causes and conditions are themselves the inconceivable Middle Way.
Regarding the principle of Buddha-nature and nirvana,
although the principle received by Bodhisattvas through this teaching is neither shallow nor profound, it is as such.
Yet, those who realize it do not lack levels of shallow and deep attainment.
Now, in clarifying the entry into the Way according to the Perfect Teaching,
it likewise possesses four gates.
First, the gate of existence;
second, the gate of emptiness;
third, the gate of both emptiness and existence.
The fourth is the gate of neither emptiness nor existence.
Although the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) possesses these four gates,
the intent of the various Mahāyāna sūtras generally employs the gate of neither emptiness nor existence to elucidate the stages.
Just as in this sutra,
although the various bodhisattvas each spoke of entering the gate of non-duality and were largely in agreement,
upon close examination, there were nonetheless distinctions among the four gates.
Yet, they most frequently employ the gate of "neither empty nor existent" to enter inconceivable liberation.
This meaning shall become self-evident below.
If one responds to conditions to benefit sentient beings according to their capacities through these four gates,
all such actions enter the inconceivable liberation;
how could one possibly employ them in a partial or biased manner?
However, for the sake of clarifying the meaning of the stages of practice and realization,
it is necessary to proceed in this manner;
therefore, I shall now clarify the sequence of stages in the Perfect Teaching.
This is explained by means of the gate of being neither empty nor existent.
Within this, there are five points:
first, distinguishing the Perfect [Teaching] from the Two Teachings; second, clarifying the differences in their stages.
Second, the explicit explanation of the stages according to the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao).
Third, the citation of various sutras and treatises as proof.
Fourth, the analytical examination.

Fifth, regarding the stages of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), this explains the meaning of "Pure Vimalakīrti. First, distinguishing between the Perfect and the two other teachings to clarify their differing stages: [The text continues: "The *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra says: 'From the first stage up to the tenth, one gradually attains the ten kinds of non-retrogression. This refers to the Bodhisattva stages. Furthermore, it says: "'The first stage is called Joyful. It is named 'Joyful' because one has attained the joy of the Dharma-nature. And so forth, up to: "'The tenth stage is called Cloud of Dharma. It is named 'Cloud of Dharma' because one rains down the great Dharma-rain upon all sentient beings. This clarifies that from the first stage through the tenth, one gradually attains the ten kinds of non-retrogression. Regarding the Bodhisattvas of the Shared Teaching (*xiangtong jiao*), it is said: "'The first stage is called Joyful. It is named 'Joyful' because one has attained the joy of the Dharma-nature. And so forth, up to: "'The tenth stage is called Cloud of Dharma. It is named 'Cloud of Dharma' because one rains down the great Dharma-rain upon all sentient beings. This clarifies that from the first stage through the tenth, one gradually attains the ten kinds of non-retrogression. Regarding the Bodhisattvas of the Distinct Teaching (*biejiao*), it is said: "'The first stage is called Joyful. It is named 'Joyful' because one has attained the joy of the Dharma-nature. Since the Perfect Teaching elucidates the perfect principle,
bodhisattvas who receive this teaching completely sever the delusions of the five abodes,
open the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, and abide in Great Nirvana.
This constitutes the perfection of teaching and the perfection of principle;
the perfection of wisdom, the perfection of abandonment, the perfection of practice, and the perfection of stages;
as well as the perfection of cause and the perfection of fruit.
The distinctions between the Separate and Complete Teachings have been explained as previously stated;
now, to further clarify the characteristics of these two teachings— Separate and Complete— I shall briefly employ five points of meaning.
First, the distinctions in the levels of attainment are determined based on the severance of ignorance;
second, the distinctions are based on the severance of views and afflictions regarding the internal and external realms;
third, the distinctions are based on what has been severed and what has not been severed.
Fourth, distinguishing the differences between the Separate and Perfect [teachings] by way of stages;
fifth, distinguishing whether the stages are common or not common.
First, distinguishing the differences in rank by way of severing ignorance:
If one follows the distinct teaching (*bipōjiào*),
the stages are explained such that upon reaching the same level as the thirty minds,
one exhausts the fetters within the realm and simultaneously suppresses the ignorance beyond the realm.
Up until the final mind-moment of dedication,
one begins to give rise to true wisdom in the first stage and sever the first grade of ignorance;
continuing in this manner until the tenth grade is severed, these are designated as the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
Only after the mind of equal enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) does ignorance cease and come to an end.
In the wondrous fruition of constant awakening (*nitya-phala*), one is serenely free from all burdens; there is nothing further to be severed.
This is as previously explained.
According to what is elucidated in the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao),
from the initial mind of sympathetic joy,
one cultivates the threefold contemplation within a single mind and enters the stage of the ten faiths (shixin).
When the afflictions within the realm of cessation are exhausted,
one simultaneously subdues the ignorance beyond that realm;
at the initial stage of the ten abodes, true wisdom is immediately awakened.
One cuts off the first grade of the ground of abiding ignorance (*avidyā-āśraya-bhūmi*).
From this point, throughout the forty stages of mind,
one continues to cut off ignorance until reaching the final moment of mind prior to equal enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Ignorance is thereby completely extinguished;
the stage of wondrous enlightenment is so solemn that it stands entirely beyond all conditioned burdens.
This is called ultimate bodhi, the unsurpassed nirvana.
This is because it distinguishes between the high and low levels [of the stages].
Thus, there are differences in the clarification of the stages between the Perfect Teaching and the Separate Teachings.
Second, regarding the difference in the severance of the views and thoughts within the realm and without the realm, as well as ignorance:
If, according to the Separate Teaching,
one severs the views and afflictions within the realm and suppresses the ignorance beyond the realm during the thirty stages of mind.
The delusions of views, thought-afflictions, and ignorance that are severed at the ten stages (daśabhūmi) beyond the realm [of the two vehicles] are divided into three paths,
as explained previously in the analysis of the ten stages within the Separate Teaching (biejiao).
As for the ten levels of faith (daśa-śraddhā) in the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao):
One cuts off the views and afflictions within the realm of the conditioned;
one perfectly subdues the views, afflictions, and ignorance beyond the realm of the conditioned,
thereby initiating the first stage of the path toward enlightenment.

The delusions of view, thought, and ignorance beyond the realm of the "perfect severance" (yuan-duan-jie) are finally exhausted only upon reaching the stage of Equal Enlightenment (Sambodhi). Therefore,
the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-śāstra* explains the "pure and purified dhyāna" (*viśuddha-viśuddha-dhyāna*) as follows:
The "pure meditation purified by being free from all views" and the "pure meditation purified by the severance of the afflictive obscurations and the cognitive obscurations"—
these both clarify the meaning of the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra states:
"Bodhisattvas of the ten stages are still turned by the delusions of the view of non-self.
This refers to the meaning that the view of annihilation has not yet been completely severed.

Yet, one attains clear realization.
These distinctions between clear and unclear realization are all based on whether the delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) have been exhausted or not;
hence the difference between clarity and lack of clarity.
Regarding the statement that "the craving for sensual desire is severed only upon reaching the fruit of Buddhahood":
the craving for sensual desire refers to the six desires.
As the Aṅgulimāla Sūtra says:
That which is called the eye-faculty is,

This applies even to the faculty of the mind (*manas*).
As stated in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* regarding the purification of the six faculties,
although one has not yet attained the outflow-free (*anāsrava*) state, [the faculties are purified].
That his six sense-faculties are thus purified should be understood as the stage of subduing the afflictions of desire and attachment;

Thus, one immediately cuts off and severs desire and attachment;

This clarifies that the six sense faculties of a Buddha are ultimately pure.
Regarding the statement that "attachment to form is severed only upon reaching Equal Enlightenment," the *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* says:

this is called liberation from form.
As for the statement that "attachment to the form of nirvāṇa is only exhausted and severed when attachment to the formless is exhausted upon reaching Buddhahood":
With the cessation of this feeling,

the same applies to perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
This is called the liberation from feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness;
it is when attachment to form has ceased that nirvana is attained.

"All dharmas are equal, and thus food is also equal.
To give a single meal to all beings—

Does this meaning differ from the previous teaching of severance and suppression in the Separate Vehicle?
The Sūtra states that one should rely on sūtras of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).

there is as yet no discussion of awakening or non-awakening;

To discuss awakening without having awakened,
and to discuss the shallow and the profound without being either shallow or profound—
search through the various Mahāyāna sūtras.
The ultimate elucidation of principle is none other than the *Avataṃsaka*, the *Mahāsaṃnipāta*, the *Mahāvaipulya*, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa*.
Although these clarify that the dharma-realm is equal, ineffable, and non-demonstrative, they do so.
Yet the practice of the Bodhisattva stage remains brilliantly manifest throughout the day;
therefore, we shall now again delineate the stages of the Bodhisattva according to the seven positions to clarify the rank of the Bodhisattva in the Perfect Teaching.
First, regarding the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*),
there are four points.
The first clarifies how faith arises from hearing the Dharma.
Second, clarifying practice based on faith;
third, clarifying entry into the stages based on practice;
fourth, clarifying the differences in the scriptural explanations.
First, regarding those who give rise to faith by hearing the Dharma:
those of superior faculties and sharp wisdom hear that the Perfect Teaching explains that the conditions and causes are themselves the Middle Way.
When one realizes the principle of the four noble truths as being without activity,
one immediately gains faith and understanding in the single truth of reality;
this is precisely the suchness, the coming and going, and the Buddha-nature of empty space.
It is neither mundane nor supramundane;
it is neither cause nor fruit;
it cannot be proclaimed and cannot be demonstrated.
To speak of the causes and effects of the mundane world without speaking is precisely the non-activity of suffering and its origin;
to speak of the causes and effects of the supramundane world is [the non-activity of cessation and the path].
This is precisely the unconditioned cessation of the path.
Therefore, in this sutra, the Great Being rebukes Maitreya, saying:
"The Buddha knows that all sentient beings are ultimately quiescent."
That which is the characteristic of nirvana cannot be extinguished further;
all sentient beings are themselves the characteristic of bodhi.
If one knows that nirvana is itself birth-and-death, [one realizes this truth].
This is the truth of suffering as being without volitional action (*anabhisaṃskāra*).
If one knows that awakening (*bodhi*) is itself affliction (*kleśa*),
this is the truth of origination as being without volitional action.
If one knows that birth and death are themselves nirvāṇa,
this is the unconditioned truth of cessation.
If one knows that afflictions are themselves bodhi.
This is the truth of the path of non-action;
it is simply neither birth-and-death nor nirvana,
neither bodhi nor affliction.
This is the single ultimate truth.
Regarding this discourse on the single ultimate truth,
these four truths are precisely the four ultimate truths of non-action.
Why is this so? It is because the four truths are elucidated by means of the one reality;
yet the one reality does not constitute the four.
Four [cases] where one does not act oneself;
four where one does not act through another;
and four where one does not act through both together.
Nor are they produced without causes and conditions;
yet they are spoken of as four,
for these are the four that are without action.
These four are ultimately unattainable;
they are the single ultimate truth,
which is called the Four Noble Truths of Non-action.
If one hears this and attains unimpeded faith and understanding,
one will immediately believe that all sentient beings are themselves the inconceivable liberation;
they are the Mahāyāna itself, and they are Prajñā itself.
This is precisely the Śūraṅgama;
it is the Buddha-nature;
it is the Dharmakāya.
This is the true mark;
this is the Middle Way, the ultimate truth;
this is the Tathāgatagarbha.
This is the dharma-realm.
This is ultimate emptiness.
This is all the Buddha-dharmas.
Therefore, the bodhicitta of compassionate vows arises;
this constitutes the faith and understanding of the "name-as-such" (myōji soku) in the Perfect Teaching.
Second, clarifying the practice based on faith:
Therefore, one who possesses the mind of faith has already generated the bodhicitta;
if they wish to practice the path of enlightenment, [they must proceed accordingly].
One should receive, uphold, recite, explain, and transcribe the Mahāyāna sūtras.
If a world-transcending practitioner wishes to swiftly enter the stage of the ten faiths and achieve the purity of the six sense faculties, [they must do so].
You should arouse diligence and not begrudge your body or life;
you ought to further cultivate the four kinds of samādhi.
Regarding the four kinds of samādhi:
the first is the samādhi of constant sitting,
as explained in the Mañjuśrī-prajñā-sūtra.
Second is the samādhi of constant walking,
as described in the *Pratyutpanna-samādhi Sūtra*.
Third is the samādhi of half-walking and half-sitting, as described in the Vaipulya sūtras such as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
The fourth is the samādhi that is neither walking nor sitting;
this refers to the various methods of practice taught in the Mahāyāna sūtras.
These are the methods of practice for these various samādhis.
This is as explained in detail throughout the various Mahāyāna sūtras;
it serves as a substitute for the initial stage of the contemplation of settling the mind.
Here, we rely upon the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao).
One should understand that when practicing the various samādhis of the initial stage of faith, one ought to have faith and resolve in ten dharmas.
As for these ten dharmas,
their names are as explained previously in the section on the three contemplations.
First, regarding those who well understand the conceivable and inconceivable causes and conditions:
as for the conceivable causes and conditions,
they are as elucidated in the aforementioned three teachings.
The inconceivable causes and conditions are precisely those now being explained:
the four true realities of the inconceivable and unconditioned.
As clarified in the previous three contemplations,
it is like a single moment of a sleeping mind that contains all phenomena;
neither vertical nor horizontal, this is precisely the inconceivable *pratyaya* (condition).
The non-actuated [truth] is the Four Noble Truths in their ultimate reality.
Thus, the Great Being Vimalakīrti rebuked Maitreya, saying:
"All sentient beings are themselves Great Nirvāṇa."
This is the characteristic of bodhi.
This inconceivable dependent origination is clarified here;
the same applies to the other nine dharmas as well.
The meaning and intent are profound and obscure;
they shall now be clarified in sequence.
Those who seek [the truth] should reflect upon them well.
The second clarifies the true awakening of the mind,
which is precisely unconditional great compassion and the four great vows of non-action.
Great compassion without conditions:
contemplating that birth-and-death is itself nirvana,
and that afflictions are themselves bodhi.
To bestow upon sentient beings this bliss of the path to cessation is the unconditioned great compassion that contemplates nirvana as being identical to saṃsāra.
Enlightenment is itself affliction;
it is for the purpose of uprooting this false accumulation of suffering for sentient beings.
This refers to the four great vows of non-action.
To know that nirvana is identical to birth-and-death is to cause those who have not yet crossed over the truth of suffering to cross over the truth of suffering.
To know that bodhi is identical to afflictions is likewise so.
It causes those who have not yet understood the Truth of Origination to understand the Truth of Origination;
it brings about the realization that afflictions are themselves bodhi.
It causes those who have not yet established themselves in the Truth of the Path to establish themselves in the Truth of the Path.
Knowing that birth and death are themselves nirvana,
they cause those who have not yet attained nirvana to attain it.
Such is the compassionate vow of the bodhisattva.
Without conditions or conceptual thought, it covers all sentient beings;
like a great cloud, it exerts no effort,
and like a magnet attracting iron— it is called the truly authentic bodhicitta.
Those who practice the path to bodhi with the three knowledges and diligently cultivate śamatha and vipaśyanā know that saṃsāra is itself nirvāṇa;
this is precisely the skillful cultivation of śamatha.
If one knows that afflictions are themselves awakening,
this is the skillful cultivation of contemplation.
It is like the harmonious balance of yin and yang, whereby all things grow and flourish.
If one skillfully cultivates śamatha and vipaśyanā, one can then single-mindedly fulfill the myriad practices.
