First, a general exposition of the sūtras and śāstras;
second, a specific exposition of the sūtras and śāstras.
Regarding the first, the general exposition of the sūtras and śāstras:
This constitutes two intentions:
first, to provide a general exposition of the Hīnayāna sūtras;
second, to provide a general exposition of the Mahāyāna sūtras.
Regarding "a general exposition of the Hīnayāna sūtras":
treatises such as the *Abhidharma*, the *Tattvasiddhi*, and the *Kun-le* are all general expositions of the Hīnayāna sūtras and śāstras; thus, the author of the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* says:
I now intend to discuss the true meaning within the Tripiṭaka.
As for those works that equally expound both the Mahāyāna sūtras and śāstras,
these include the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-śāstra*, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*, the *Dvādaśamukha-śāstra*, and others.
These both generally present the two distinct categories— the Separate and the Perfect— clarified in the various Mahāyāna sūtras.
Second, as for the specific presentation of the sūtras and śāstras,
there are two intended meanings.
First, a separate exposition of the Hīnayāna sūtras;
second, a separate exposition of the Mahāyāna sūtras.
Regarding the first, the separate exposition of the Hīnayāna sūtras:
Just as the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* separately expounds the Sūtras,
the *Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī* (or *Vyākhyāyukti*) separately expounds the Vinaya,
and the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* and *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* separately expound the Abhidharma taught by the Buddha during his lifetime.
Second, regarding the specific application of Mahāyāna sūtras and śāstras:
for example, the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* specifically applies the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* to the two teachings of Distinct and Perfect;
the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* specifically applies the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* to the three teachings of Shared, Distinct, and Perfect.
There should be separate expositions for the *Mahāsaṃnipāta Vaipulya* and this sutra and its treatise;
they did not come to this land.
The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Śāstra* provides a separate exposition of the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
The *Dharmapada-śāstra* separately expounds the single, perfect teaching (*ekayāna*) of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*,
while the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-śāstra* separately expounds the four teachings and five flavors of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*.
These treatises do not exhaustively cover the [doctrines] of this land.
Expositions such as these that elucidate the sutras are,
in fact, expositions of the contemplation of the mind;
these various sutras are now clearly revealed.
This is precisely the diligent cultivation of the contemplation of the mind,
through which one thoroughly understands all sutras and treatises.
If the sutras and treatises did not emerge from the mind, [they would be nothing more than empty words].
If a practitioner of contemplation neither hears nor reads [the teachings],
how can they attain penetration within their own mind?
This constitutes a formal discourse that is in profound accord with the sūtras and śāstras;
such is the intended meaning here.
Second, to correctly clarify the application of the four teachings to provide a general explanation of this sutra,
it is said that "text and meaning" consists of two points:
first, the explanation of the five meanings of the sutra.
The second part corresponds to the scriptural text.
First, regarding the explanation of the five meanings of this sutra:
this is precisely as previously explained, correlating the name "Vimalakīrti" (Pure and Stainless Renown) with the stages of the four teachings.
The names are identical, but their meanings differ.
Next, regarding the clarification of the essence:
that which is elucidated by the three teachings is precisely the essence of the liberation of conceptual deliberation.
That which is elucidated in the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) is precisely the inconceivable liberation (*acintya-vimokṣa*).
Next, to clarify the fundamental principle (*zong*):
this refers to how the four teachings elucidate the four kinds of Four Noble Truths (*catur-āryasatya*), through which the causes and effects of attaining the Buddha-lands differ.
Next, to clarify their function:
this refers to the four teachings arranged from shallow to deep,
wherein each subsequent, deeper teaching progressively critiques the preceding, shallower one.
Next, regarding the classification of the doctrinal characteristics:
this sutra fully elucidates the four teachings;
it shares commonalities with other sutras, yet also possesses differences.
As analyzed previously,
there are three points regarding the interpretation of this scriptural passage by means of the four teachings and their two functions.
First, four categories that apply to the exterior of the room;
second, six categories that apply to the interior of the room;
third, four categories that apply to exiting the room.
Regarding the four categories of the exterior:
because the four teachings clarify the differences in cause and effect,
Śākyamuni manifests different Buddha-lands accordingly.
Just as Śāriputra and the Brahmā King perceived things differently,
so too do the various devas share a single precious vessel for food,
yet each receives according to their own karmic retribution.
Because the color of the rice differs,
and because they have received the four teachings differently,
they perceive the Buddha-lands as being different.
The "Exposition on the Chapter on Expedient Means" correctly employs the teachings of the Tripitaka and the Shared Teaching. Why is this so?
It explains that by deconstructing phenomena, one enters emptiness through the causes and conditions of arising and ceasing in impermanence;
it further explains the intent of entering emptiness through the provisional nature of things being like dreams and illusions.
Thus, within the causal stage, both the crude and the subtle methods are employed.
One breaks through the mind of attachment to craving and views within that realm and diligently cultivates the Dharma-body of the two teachings.
The "Chapter on Disciples" employs the Shared Teaching, the Distinct Teaching, and the Perfect Teaching.
He rebukes the ten great disciples and five hundred arhats by means of the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-yāna*).
As for this rebuke using the Shared Teaching,
it is like his criticism of Kātyāyana for explaining the three baskets (*tripiṭaka*) through the five meanings of "inept deliverance" (*duḥkhapratipad*).
To employ the Separate Teaching for refutation and censure is like [the Buddha] reproaching Pūrṇa by placing foul food in a precious vessel.
To employ the Perfect Teaching is as follows:
As the Venerable Subhūti, the "Emanated Body," said:
"Without arising from the meditative concentration of cessation,
he manifests all manner of dignified postures."
One does not cease or abandon craving;
one gives rise to clear knowledge and liberation,
neither bound nor unbound.
This is a critique made from the perspective of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao).
In the explanation of the "Bodhisattva Chapter" according to the four teachings,
it is precisely the Perfect Teaching that is employed.

First, it is explained how the Four Great Bodhisattvas employ the partial methods of the Tripiṭaka, Common, and Distinct Teachings for their own practice and for transforming others, as well as the inconceivable, perfect, and sudden path of the Lotus Sūtra.
Second, it clarifies how the four teachings are used within the "In the Room" chapter to explain the textual passages of the six chapters of the sūtra.
The Great Being has no affliction of the three teachings;
yet, through skillful means, he manifests as if sharing those three afflictions.
It is with reference to this that the inquiry regarding his illness is explained.
The "Chapter on the Inconceivable" (Fǎn'ǐyì Pǐn) clearly elucidates the manifestation of the four teachings within the inconceivable realm of the Perfect Teaching (Yuánjiào).
The "Chapter on Contemplating Sentient Beings" (Guān Zhòngshēng Pǐn) specifically distinguishes how both the Separate (Bié) and Perfect (Yuán) Teachings enter emptiness from the conventional (jiǎ).

The "Chapter on the Buddha-way" (Buddhadharmapada) precisely elucidates how the inconceivable Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao) enters from emptiness into the provisional (kaijia), practicing within non-ways to attain penetration into the Buddha-way.

The "Chapter on the Dharma-gate of Non-duality" (Fenpufa men pin) correctly clarifies how the inconceivable Middle Way of the Perfect Teaching, through correct contemplation, enters the Dharma-gate of non-duality.

The "Chapter on Fragrant Accumulation" (Gandhavyūha-parivarta) is precisely the manifestation of the dual illumination of the two truths and the perfect fusion of the dharma-realm as elucidated by the Inconceivable Perfect Teaching (Acintya-vaipulya).
The three chapters and four teachings that collectively emerge from the chamber constitute the textual content of these four chapters of the sutra.
This chapter, "The Universal Practice of Bodhisattva Conduct," causes bodhisattvas to universally practice the conduct of the four teachings and to transform sentient beings within the four lands.
Regarding the four teachings that universally apply to the "Chapter on Akṣobhya":
this clarifies that if one relies upon the four teachings to cultivate the four practices and arouse the bodhicitta.
One first attains birth in the land of Akṣobhya Buddha;
by means of this, one also accomplishes the practice for the buddha-field of the Tathāgata Akṣobhya. When one attains buddhahood, [one shall likewise establish such a realm].
All Buddha-lands are like the world of Abhirati.
As for the two chapters concerning the entrustment of the Dharma through the four teachings and the offering of the Dharma,
they are entrusted to Śakra and Maitreya.
This ensures that after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, this sutra shall circulate widely.
The four teachings benefit future disciples so that they may never cease.
